title.rendered: Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired) by Susan Jeremy

content.rendered:
Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired) by Susan Jeremy

By Edward Kliszus

Susan Jeremy’s Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired), performed at New York City’s iconic La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club, is an extraordinary one-woman show that transforms life’s job-related ups and downs into a witty, heartfelt exploration of resilience, self-discovery, and humor. With vivid characters, musical interludes, and reflections on work, dating, and personal growth, Jeremy creates a performance that is laugh-out-loud hilarious and deeply touching.

Here’s Susan Jeremy talking about her final show at LA MAMA.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Susan Jeremy (@comicjeremy)

Credit: A post shared by Susan Jeremy (@comicjeremy)

A Career Full of Colorful Stories

Jeremy’s performance is a comedic journey through her professional life, starting as a babysitter and spanning an eclectic mix of roles, including working as a bakery clerk, in food prep at Arthur Treacher’s Fish and Chips, and ushering at Radio City Music Hall. Each story is punctuated by witty one-liners, reflecting the universal struggles of navigating jobs and life’s detours.

Her stint as “Calvin Clown,” a character created for Bar Mitzvahs and children’s parties, highlights her knack for physical comedy and theatrical flair. Jeremy also reflects on her unconventional jobs, including roller-skating to sell Virginia Slims cigarettes in Los Angeles. Throughout, her mother’s advice to “get a job with a pension” serves as a humorous refrain that underscores her life’s balancing act between passion and practicality.

Character Work: A Kaleidoscope of Voices

Jeremy’s standout ability to embody various characters adds immense depth to her storytelling. A particularly poignant moment is her imitation of her grandparent’s brogue, delivered with a mix of warmth and comedic timing that captures the character’s essence.

Jeremy brings many personas to life, from mimicking colleagues and customers to adopting regional accents like the Jersey-style Sopranos twang. These impressions are not just comedic but deeply empathetic, offering insights into the people who have shaped her professional journey.

Susan Jeremy in a scene from Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired) at LA MAMA. Photo by Will Chichak. Courtesy susanjeremy.net

Studio 54: A Timepiece of Humor and Dating

One of the most memorable segments involves Jeremy’s comedic take on Studio 54, the iconic New York nightclub. She uses this setting as a nostalgic cultural timepiece and a humorous lens into her dating escapades during the disco era.

Her physical comedy shines in this segment as she recounts her experiences on the dance floor with exaggerated movements and sharp timing. This clever blend of humor and self-reflection encapsulates her ability to find levity in life’s awkward and defining moments.

Humor Meets Humanity: Teaching and Growth

While much of the show is lighthearted, Jeremy’s reflections on her time as a substitute teacher in a psychiatric ward and later as a special education teacher in New York City add a layer of emotional depth. These stories showcase her ability to find humor in challenging situations while remaining sensitive to the gravity of her work.

Her teaching career is filled with anecdotes highlighting the resilience required to thrive in public education. From navigating challenging classrooms to connecting with students, Jeremy’s experiences are relatable to educators and anyone who has faced high-stakes workplace pressures. Her journey from substitute teacher to earning an MA is a testament to her dedication and adaptability.

Susan Jeremy in a scene from Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired) at LA MAMA. Photo by Will Chichak.

A Full-Circle Moment: Retiring into Adventure

After 24 years as a teacher, Jeremy’s decision to retire and take Robert Will Show You the Door on an international tour feels like a triumphant new chapter. Her reflections on this transition underscore the themes of reinvention and self-discovery that permeate the show.

Jeremy’s ability to turn setbacks—like being fired—into opportunities for growth and creativity is inspiring. By reframing challenges as steps in her journey, she delivers a message of hope and resilience that resonates with audiences of all backgrounds.

Final Thoughts

Susan Jeremy’s “Robert Will Show You the Door (Tales of Being Fired)” is a masterful blend of comedy, storytelling, and emotional depth. Her vivid characters, sharp wit, and universal themes make this show a must-see for fans of solo performance and great theater. Whether laughing at her humorous take on Studio 54 or reflecting on the trials of public education, audiences leave the performance entertained, inspired, and deeply moved.

Readers may also enjoy Woman on a Ledge, King Lear: Tragedy in a Masterpiece Setting, and Little House on the Ferry: The Musical.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Who doesn’t want perfection?

Death Becomes Her is completely over the top, exaggerated, and extravagant. But as ridiculous as some of its moments seem, we are forced to consider just how accurate this desire for perfection, the gaze of others, our fascination and addiction to body manipulation. Our longing to have attention, to be attractive, to stop aging—at this day and age, to prevent aging altogether. This cult classic movie adaptation to stage is ever true as it was in 1992 when Meryl Streep played Madeline, a fading Hollywood star. This stage performance captures the embodiment of middle-aged women doing anything in their power–and beyond–to achieve and maintain “ideal” features. 

“It is life’s ultimate cruelty, isn’t it? To give us a precious few years of youth and beauty and then force us to witness our own decay,” Viola Van Horn (Michelle Williams) begins this performance on a spooky, dark tone. She points to someone in the audience. But it catches all our attentions–we are suddenly entangled in the shortcomings we see in ourselves.

If you think about the time and money, emotion and stress and anxiety that goes into your own appearance, the performance suddenly doesn’t seem so exaggerated. Still though, it’s hilarious. Laughable to the point where nearly every line of dialogue and song is comical. Death Becomes Her is intentional, which allows me to buy into the over the top comedy and violence and lack of limits. It is skillfully done.

Madeline (Megan Hilty), a Hollywood star, and Helen (Jennifer Simard), a writer waiting for her big break, have been best friends forever, but Madeline has always managed to steal Helen’s thunder. They love the moments they can share in laughter, but what they might love even more is an opportunity to one-up each other.

Helen finally gets that chance when she proudly introduces her fiance, Ernest Menville (Christopher Sieber), a word-renowned plastic surgeon (with good intentions to his career as he helps kids with cleft palates).

“Did you see her

When she saw us?

I could feast on that for days”

Cue Revenge.

For a second, I think she’ll get the guy, but we know that’d be too easy. In a society where physical appearance is prioritized, naturally, Ernest falls into Madeline’s trap. Just like every other guy she’s already stolen from Helen, Madeline will win again. And this man, is exactly what Madeline needs: her own personal plastic surgeon.

Helen spirals.

Ten years pass.

The quiet, undervalued, but funny, servantship of Stefan (Josh Lamon) highlights Madeline’s unwavering ego, even as her appearance and fame diminishes.

Her career is fading. So is her complexion, her hair, the gaze of others.

Cue Helen: a freshly successful writer with a newly released, impressive memoir, and a new body—one that trumps the aging Madeline.

How’s she look so fresh, so suddenly?

Cue Revenge, again.

Cue Viola Van Horn: a queen of the stage, of beauty, of vocals, and most importantly, of granting the wishes of those who would give anything to remain beautiful for eternity. She opens the show, and she closes the show.

Though, I am most—and immediately, from the rise of the curtain to the final bows— captivated by the costuming. Sequins, feathers, and everything in between—every show stopper design—is on stage. Styles change in seconds from skimp to classy to flamboyant to spooky to showstopping, as quickly and as masterfully as the sets themselves. 

The entire night, and for what I’m sure will be weeks after, I’m thinking about these costumes.

The costuming and choreography alone would bring me back again. 

Perhaps, all of this is, too, over the top enough that it makes this show such theater. It makes me buy into the loudness of its entirety. Taurean Everett (Chagall), Viola’s servant, is a standout in this show–along with the other cult groupies of Viola. The seductive, dramatic costuming. It was like I was watching Rocky Horror Picture Show meshed with class and spook and a stage full of show girls.

Photo Credit: Matthew Murphy & Evan Zimmerman

Wouldn’t you just die to look so alive?

Perfection at your fingertips

But like any level of beauty, it needs to be maintained. Beauty can still peel and chip away.  

The two women battle it out—literally—guns and ridiculously laughable tumbles down the stairs and gaping holes straight through the stomach. Again, Ernest’s services is required. He even gets the whole stage to himself for this number—now our gaze is on Ernest.

Fifty years pass…will anyone end up happy? Will they have that a-ha moment where they realize that…that they want an ending?

Photo Credit: Matthew Murphy & Evan Zimmerman

CAST: Megan Hilty (Madeline Ashton), Jennifer Simard (Helen Sharp), Christopher Sieber (Ernest Menville), Michelle Williams (Viola Van Horn), Josh Lamon (Stefan)

Ensemble: Marija Abney (Counselor), Lauren Celentano (Woman #1), Sarita Colon, Kaleigh Cronin (Stacey), Natalie Charle Ellis (Nurse #1), Taurean Everett (Chagall), Michael Graceffa (Chance), Neil Haskell (Priest), Kolton Krouse (Silks Dance), Sarah Meahl (Sarah), Ximone Rose (Woman #2), Sir Brock Warren (Minister), Bud Weber (Doctor), Ryan Worsing (Director), Warren Yang.

Swings: Kyle Brown, Lakota Knuckle, Johanna Moise, and Amy Quanbeck.

Directed and Choreographed by Tony Award winner Christopher Gattelli.

Death Becomes Her features a book by Marco Pennette; Original score by Julia Mattison and Noel Carey.

CREATIVE TEAM: Derek McLane (Scenic Design), Paul Tazewell (Costume Design), Justin Townsend (Lighting Design), Peter Hylenski (Sound Design), Charles LaPointe (Hair & Wig Design), Joe Dulude II (Make-Up Design), Cha Ramos (Fight Direction), Mary-Mitchell Campbell(Music Supervision), Doug Besterman (Orchestrations), Ben Cohn (Music Direction), Sam Davis (Dance & Music Arrangements), Mary-Mitchell Campbell, Julia Mattison and Noel Carey (Vocal Arrangements), and Kristy Norter (Music Coordination).

Death Becomes Her opened Nov. 21 at Lunt-Fontanne Theatre, 205 W 46th St, New York, NY 10036. Run time is two and a half hours, including a 15-minute intermission. Tickets are on sale through August 2025.

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Abby (Marisa Tomei) and Gus (Arliss Howard) have worked at A&R records for decades; they’re connected both personally and professionally by experience and experiences. Now, there’s a new hire—Katherine (Gracie McGraw), who is making Abby and Gus face questions they had no interest in facing: questions about power, abuse, and responsibility. 

The heart of the story is the power dynamics; Gus is the boss and he says what’s on his mind. And he has a lot on his mind. He rants and rages—insulting and belittling everyone around him. And yet he’s smart! He’s good at what he does. So, the play asks: What is the price of genius? And who pays? It goes on to raise another important question: whose responsibility is it to apologize? I wish it had probed a little deeper at the questions, asked more about ethical obligation—to friendship, to genius. The show did leave questions on the table, questions that I wish it had explored. 

One of my favorite parts of the play was that Gracie McGraw doesn’t just play Katherine—but also transforms into Kat Wonder, the superstar and Abby’s love interest, someone Abby feels responsible for both creating and destroying. Gracie McGraw transitions between characters, from the nervous and over-eager Katherine into the bold and confident Kat; these transitions serve as a reminder of the power and pain of love and illusion. 

The way Katherine reminds Abby of Kat is both painful and beautiful to see. When she becomes Kat, you can see Abby join her, flying back in time, becoming younger, energetic, joyful, free. And then Kat returns to Katherine—and you can see Abby’s disappointment. I love the beauty of how hard it can be to separate past and present, real love from imitation. The relationship between Abby and Kat—this love story and friendship and artistic development—it’s nostalgic, compelling, and lovely. 

What I wish we had seen was more of the past, more of Abby and Gus’ past. The reality is that what keeps Abby and Gus attached to each other, what keeps them going—is their past. What is true now is a faint remnant of what was true. Their past, their history–it gives their relationship depth, weight, and meaning. Unfortunately, the play spends much more time on this present, robbing us of the opportunity to relate to their shared history, to understand what keeps them together. By focusing on the present more than the past, we don’t quite see why exactly Abby is so attached to Gus, what he means to her, why she stays despite the abuse and neglect. The heart of the story, what truly propels it along…is missing.

Babe raises important questions, but misses opportunities to push those questions further. However, the cast is fabulous–from Marisa Tomei’s snarky glances to Arliss Howard’s ease in creating tension to Gracie McGraw’s incredible singing.

Babe is limited Off-Broadway engagement at The Pershing Square Signature Center until December 22, 2024. You can buy tickets here.

title.rendered: Ann Hampton Callaway and Liz Callaway: New York State of Mind

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The Callaway Sisters are back together in New York City and sharing their loves and lives for only a short time: November 26-30 (including a special Thanksgiving Day performance at 8PM). If you have a chance to take some time off from the turkey (or go all-in on the Thursday show), this is an ideal way to step away from the table, gift yourself some blessings, and share in the love emanating from the stage at 54 Below.

Fluidly backed up by Ritt Henn on bass, Ron Tierno on drums, and their music director Alex Rybeck on piano, the love is four-fold, of New York, of singing together, of their audience, and of sisterhood. This combination makes for a rock solid, thoughtful, touching, and full evening. The two of them bring a long history of singing and their experiences in showbusiness that add substance to each one of their song choices.

There’s something about being older and having lived a full life that brings a weight and a depth to this performance and endows it with a richness that can only be had from having lived that life. That something is prominent in this performance, and coupled with the intimacy of sisterhood, makes for an ever so delightful evening. Many performers can bring their talent to the stage, but only a few are also able to simultaneously give it to the audience at the same time.

Between them they have these accolades: Tony Award nominees, Emmy winner, Grammy nominee, multi-platinum-selling pop/jazz singer-songwriter recently inducted into the Women Songwriters Hall of Fame. Ann’s compositions have been recorded and performed by Melissa Manchester, Carole King, Patti Lupone, Liza Minnelli, Barbara Streisand, and Michael Feinstein.

Originally from Chicago, but having lived their formative years in New York, their set list reflects the love of what the city has given to them in their careers. “New York State of Mind,” of course, followed by a fun medley of songs they sang together on car trips to annoy their parents, flowing to a most lovely duet of “That’s the Way I’ve Always Heard It Should Be,” the tongue tripper “Cloudburst,” and Ann’s composition “Remind Me.” They each step aside to let the other solo, with Ann singing “My Buddy” and “Blowin in the Wind” as a poignant protest song for today, and Liz delivering “Meadowlark” (a song she sang at her first singing/waitress job oh so many years ago) and the heart wrenching “I’ll Be Here.” They close with Cole Porter’s “I Happen to Like New York,” and following a standing ovation, encore with “Count Your Blessings.”

Liz and Ann exude obvious joy in singing together and sharing their music and stories. “We were truly blessed and are truly grateful,” they say. We feel the same having shared the evening with them.

—-

“Ann Hampton Callaway and Liz Callaway: New York State of Mind” THROUGH NOVEMBER 30 – at 54 Below. 254 W 54TH ST. CELLAR, NYC 10019

Tickets can be purchased here.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

We Live in Cairo is a generational yearning for change;

six artists come together and they use their artistic talents and passion to fight for change, for freedom, for a future.

We Live in Cairo is the culmination of a decade of development.

“You see Tunisia

You hear of riots

You live in Cairo so you feel it

I feel it too

What do we do?”

Beginning in February 2010, one year before the revolution, we are immersed into one day to the next, the days counted on the stage’s back wall.

As a new president is set to take office, The Muslim Brotherhood takes the Parliament, and the group of youth fears they will also take the presidency. We Live in Cairo centers on the youth’s political opposition and the violence and rage surrounding the Brotherhood.

Amir (Ali Louis Bourzgui), a musician, and his brother, Hany (Michael Khalid Karadsheh), a writer, are both Christians. They prepare songs for Amir to perform in the city’s square. Layla (Nadina Hassan), is introduced to us as ‘s girlfriend—as she is also introduced to the other young artists. On several occasions, Layla claims to not be political, but it doesn’t take long for her actions to tell there’s been a brave switch. About halfway through the play, she is fighting alongside Fadwa (Rotana Tarabzouni), activist and fearless leader of the group. I’m not sure what moment or experience shaped this transition, but I would have loved to see it.

Photo Credit: Joan Marcus

Karim (John El-Jor), a visual artist in his medium of graffiti, is Fadwa’s well-off cousin, with a backdrop of drugs and alcohol playing into his silly and lively personality. The entry point where we really come to know him is one of the most prominent in both character development and context for both the group’s political views and point in history. His satirical puppetry has the audience in complete laughter–the most and perhaps only humorous scenes of the performance–

Karim takes on Hassan (Drew Elhamalawy), an outsider, as an apprentice. The songs and set surrounding moments when Karim and Hassan are making satirical art are noteworthy as we move from night to day and risking it all to take a stand.

For a two and a half hour production, I expected to really gain an understanding of these characters compared to the level of with which I left the theater. Since the artists’ passion is so strong, I wanted more backstory. Besides their artistry and participation in the revolution, we know little. How did they all find each other and create this safe, “gallery” space in which we spend so much of the evening?

Fadwa is the most developed. I wonder about these students’ parents. Hassan’s father is the only character whose parent is semi-present throughout the play through worried and angry phone calls, warning and arguing with his son, disagreeing with his choice of friends and decisions. We understand that Fawda comes from a family of strong beliefs; she herself has already been imprisoned. We live in Cairo begins as Fadwa is released from prison and is reunited with her friends—and the idea of her returning to jail–or a worse punishment–doesn’t stop her from her fight.

The score does significant work—perhaps more than the performance aside. Songs remind us where we are, they tell the surroundings we don’t see from the stage, they tell us about whats going on around us, narrate the difficult images we only imagine through headlines projected over the stage and ceilings.

The set is powerful, the most impactful aspect of this play; at one point we see a graphic image–having already been warned of content–by which I’m surprised. It helps us to better understand the intensity of the circumstances, feel the honesty of these true, recent events in history.

“We have cracked the wall of fear…”

In June 2012, Mohamed Morsi, candidate of the Brotherhood is elected. What the six youth fought so hard to stop–

An intermission separates the time before the revolution and the time post-revolution.

We watch as they are given opportunities to leave Egypt—who will stay, who will leave? Is leaving abandoning your home, even if it no longer feels safe; even if a future feels lost?

I’m waiting for death; it seems impossible to avoid, especially as they place themselves at the center of riots—sometimes being the first and only ones there. They spearhead meetings, protests, stand-ins. They use social media to reach others and are often successful in their efforts.

As the young adults carve their own paths, their hope for revolution doesn’t leave. We finally see the results, the consequences, the closure. We Live in Cairo is the strength of one voice; how one loud voice can build to change.

“I was one person

Wh had an idea

Who made it words

And someone heard

Someone heard…”

Photo Credit: Joan Marcus

Books, Music, & Lyrics by The Lazours.

Choreography & Movement Direction by Ann Yee.

Directed by Taibi Magar.

CREATIVE TEAM:

Tilly Grimes (Scenic Design), Dina El-Aziz (Costume Design), Bradley King (Lighting Design), Justin Stasiw (Sound Design), David Bengali (Projection Design), Daniel Lazour & Michael Starobin (Orchestrations), Madeline Benson (Vocal Arrangements & Music Supervisor), Mona Seyed-Bolorforosh (Music Director), Xavier Clark (Voice & Text Coach), Raphael Mishler (Puppet Design), Jon Knust (Properties Supervisor), Claire Yenson (Casting), Jeff Brancato (Production Stage Manager).

We Live in Cairo opened October 27, 2024 at New York Theatre Workshop after making its world premiere at American Repertory Theater in 2019. The performance runs two hours and thirty minutes with one 15-minute intermission.

Sophia Alawi (Understudy), Ali Louis Bourzgui (Amir), Travis Darghali (Understudy), Drew Elhamalawy (Hassan), John El-Jor (Karim), Nadina Hassan (Layla), Michael Khalid Karadsheh (Hany), Rotana Tarabzouni (Fadwa).

content.rendered:
By Tulis mcCall

The cast of Bedlam‘s “Music CIty” does not give you a chance to not fall in love with them.  Not one ounce of a chance.  If you get your butt in a seat in this cozy theatre, they claim your heart as theirs.  Fair and Square.

You looking for a spectaular way to spend a couple of hours that will lift you up and fill you with a joyoful noise?  Look no further.  Take it from me – you don’t want to miss this one.  I wish we had more than 5 stars for rating productions. J.T. Harding and Peter Zinn have created a production that is a master class in how to weave harmony and story, and this superb cast, under the direction of Eric Tucker, delivers the goods.

First of all I arrived on time, and this meant I was late.  The show starts before it starts with music and an open mic (so I heard tell).  The setting is a ficticious bar called The Wicked Tickle located in the Nowhere section of Nashville.  Every night is open mic night and our hosts are Wyn (Julianne B. Merrill), Drew (Jonathan Judge-Russo) and his brother TJ (Stephen Michael Spencer).  On the night in question the bar is visited by Leanne (Leenya Rideout), a scout looking for new songs for her clients to cover.  She likes what Drew and TJ are dishing out and wants a demo.

Which, of course, these fellas don’t have.  Nor do they have the money for a session ($3,000).  They do have the recording engineer.  All they need is the money.

So begins the saga.

Their quest takes them across the path of Bakerman (Andrew Rothenberg) who is busy producing batches of his drug-laced cookes and other such products – that maybe include sex with anyone passing by.  He is in need of dlivery boys.  For which he pays handsomely.  No problem – just a little guilt, but the show must go on.  The problem DOES come when TJ’s path leads to Tammy (Leenya Rideout), the mother of the latest open mic phenom “23” (named in the style of a Get Smart cohort) (Casey Shuler).  TJ has taken a shine to 23 both artistically and romantically and, well, he is soon sorely tested.

Plots beget more plots including a semi-menacing presence of Stucky Stiles (Andrew Rothenberg) who knows a good song when hears one and is willing to bust up any team in his way in order to grab it.

Romance, music, poverty, drugs and even life and death swirl thought these characters’s as well as their music.  They may be fiction but these excellent performers represent the sea of artists of every medium who put their lives into their work and their work into our world.  The musicianship here is top notch with nearly every actor playing at least one instrument and every single one blending in harmonies that shake you down to where you live.

I cannot single out one performace as the focal point of this tale.  Each person has moments that are close to being transcendant.  So treat yourself and enjoy this spectacular cornucopia.

BEDLAM presents the New York Premier of Music City: A New Musical – music and lyrics by J.T. Harding, book by Peter Zinn; Eric Tucker (director)

WITH Drew Bastian, Corry J. Ethridge, Julianne B. Merrill, Leenya Rideout, Andrew Rothenberg, Jonathan Judge-Russo, Casey Shuler, Stephen Michael Spencer, Holly Wilder.

 Musicians include Ann Klein (guitar) and Tony Tino (bass).

John Heginbotham(choreographer), Julianne Merrill(WYN/Music Supervisor and Director), Clifton Chadick (set design), Daniele Tyler Mathews (costume designer), Jane Shaw (sound designer), and Buffy Cardoza (props/associate set designer).

At West End Theater, THROUGH December 22.  263 West 86 Street.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

As you walk into The Merchant of Venice (originally entitled The most excellent historie of the Merchant of Venice with the exxtreame cruelitie of Shylocke the Jewe) now playing at Classic Stage Company, you realize after a few minutes that you have become a member of the television studio audience here to see cable-access’s own The Antonio Show!!!! A show filled with Fun, Romance, and Comedy (“Why are chickens afraid of Shakespeare? Well, you’d be scared too, if he wanted to “MURDER most FOWL!”) as they present, for the studio audience and those at home, their The Play That Goes Wrong version of William Shakespeare‘s classic antisemitic play. Actors have left, crew have revolted, things aren’t ready, but the show must go on, 5-4-3-2-1, and cue.

Your host for the evening, Antonio (a charismatic T.R. Knight), begins in a talk-show format, interviewing puppets and other actors, to lay out where we’re at. We’re in Venice ensconced in the world of traders that send out ships around the world to both buy and sell goods. If all works out, an initial investment can be recouped six fold+. But if it doesn’t, you’re busted.

In need of funds for a new venture, upstanding member of the community, Antonio, comes to usurer Shylock to borrow. Shylock, not being part of the inner circle, is surprised at the request and in the terms of the contract, adds a clause that if the debt is not paid by a certain date, he may extract an actual pound of Antonio’s flesh. Pretty harsh. Antonio laughs at the request – thinking his ship will come in – and signs. Of course, the ship doesn’t come in and we’re headed to crash on the rocks and the tragic end of the play.

In betweenst this plot is the love, lust, and romance of the citizens of Venice, the unicorns, superheros, bubble machines, rap songs, x-rated puppets, and haunting renditions of Stand By Me, and Sometimes When We Touch (beautifully sung by Noah Pacht).

Richard Topol, as Shylock, brings the personal pain of the character to the forefront, the loneliness, the degradation, and the spit-upon. He begins the play as an average business man-among-many and is quickly transformed by the other characters and costumed in a Dracula cape, spiked vampire teeth, large Groucho nose and glasses, and a blood stained shirt. He conforms to their wishes and goes all out in giving them what they want. Their making of him in their image grants them, in essence, what they deserve come the end of the play. Do we have input in the creation of our own enemies?

Director Igor Golyak has created a Merchant of Venice reflective of our modern time, busy, entertaining, titillating, short on attention span, flippant, with the sense-of-it-all just below the surface

At times this carnival atmosphere is so bright and shiny, it becomes a distraction and the edifice of frivolity has to be broken in order to fit-in the sidebar of the seriousness of this play.

Shakespeare is so revered today because his work is so universal, transcending eras as it speaks of the human condition. And we absolutely need to be spoken to. This adaptation is both entertaining and poignant in its morality.

—–

The Merchant of Venice by William Shakespeare, Adapted and directed by Igor Golyak

The cast includes Richard Topol, Alexandra Silber, Gus Birney, José Espinosa, Tess Goldwyn, Stephen Ochsner, T.R. Knight, Noah Pacht, and muscian Fedor Zhuravlev.

Jan Pappelbaum, Scenic Design; Sasha Ageeva, Costume & Props Design; Seth Reiser, Lighting Design; Fedor Zhuravlev, Sound Design & Composer; Igor Golyak, Projections Design; Timur Sadykov, Hair and Makeup Design; and Leana Gardella, Fight and Intimacy Consultant.

Running Time: 2 hours 10 minutes with no intermission.  At Classic Stage Company through December 22.

Tickets can be bought HERE.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

This is a story of four sisters and one next generation woman told in large swaths.  Katori Hall writes well and often about people who have deep history invested in one another (The Hot Wing King was a brilliant play that opened weeks before the pandemic and closed way too soon).  She digs deep and takes no prisoners.  Lileana Blain-Cruz is the Resident Director at Lincoln Center Theatre and appreciates the idea of challenging the audience to sit up and lean in.  All in all an impressive team.

This story of four sisters is unique and universal.  They meet on an island off the coast of Georgia where their family has lived for generations.  Decades – perhaps centuries – of history are found in the quilts with which these women grew up.  Quilts were the one constant on which they could depend.  If I get this correctly (the details are a bit sketchy) each of the sisters was fathered by a different man, and each of these men disappointed their mother.  All that is left of them is a collection of stories and some important memorabilia, including the quilts them selves.

Clementine (Crystal Dickinson) is the sister who stayed home to care for their mother (recently deceased).  Gio (Adrienne C. Moore) is a local cop filled with beer and resentment.  Cassan (Susan Kelechi Watson) is an army medic and mother of the unpredictable Zambia (Mirirai).  Amber (Lauren E. Banks) is the one who got away and became a hot lawyer for famous folks.

Amber is also the one delegated by their mother to read THE WILL about which no one knew.  It is the reading of the will that sets this family into a royal tailspin.  Clementine will stand against any change that pulls them away from their heritage while the rest will have plenty to say and argue as the story reveals itself.

As a whole, this production is a bit of a jumble.  Staging is awkward, dialogue overlaps and is easily missed, and the story wanders.  While the first act is relatively tight, the second act takes off for parts unknown and tries to include so much that we lose the thread of the story.  As the tale reaches it’s conclusion there are a series of “one more thing” elements that feel unsupported.  This is exquisite ensemble work, but that is not quite enough to keep us buoyed until the final final.

THE BLOOD QUILT by Katori Hall, directed by Lileana Blain-Cruz.

WITH Lauren E. Banks, Crystal Dickinson, Mirirai, Adrienne C. Moore, and Susan Kelechi Watson.

THE BLOOD QUILT features sets by Adam Rigg, costumes by Montana Levi Blanco, lighting by Jiyoun Chang, sound by Palmer Hefferan, and projections by Jeanette Oi-Suk Yew. Theresa Flanagan is the Stage Manager.

At Lincoln Center Theater.  Through December 29th.  Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

You wouldn’t necessarily know it by the way he presents himself on the stage, but Sam Kissajukian has held six solo exhibitions of his artwork.  An artist who got his start as a stand-up comedian and decided to explore painting for the first time at the age of 36, his paintings are quirky and playful, while also being vulnerable and wide-ranging in style; his art very much matches his stage presence, as he tells the story of his journey to becoming an “artist.”

The piece starts in what seems like a stand-up comedy routine, with Kissajukian putting himself on the chopping block while holding an awareness of the harm that making oneself the butt of the joke can take (and did with him).  What this leads into is a vulnerable (yet still humorous) look at what was needed to break apart from this identity and find a place of understanding and embracing the many aspects (and states of being) of himself, through art.

As Kissajukian breaks with his performative existence of constantly seeking acceptance and approval, he falls into a five month manic episode where he creates 300 Paintings.  In the piece, playing at the Vineyard Theatre through December 15, Sam catalogs the series of wild artistic endeavors, showcasing the artwork that resulted.  In addition to the many paintings he created, he also embarked on other artistic endeavors, questioning the nature of art, business, dreams, and mental stability.  Kissajukian turns the societal standards of art and business on their head and I couldn’t help but think – this is genius – as he countered his unwavering confidence by teasing himself for his unstable mental state at the time.  We laugh along the way, but what Kissajukian shows us is something refreshingly creative and unusually original –  much like himself and the art he makes.  Perhaps it takes an unconventional mind to put a mirror up to not only the artist’s internal monologue, but the shared experience of humanity.  

During the latter half of the piece, Kissajukian leads us along his path to discovery of having bipolar.  He realizes that his paintings and visual artwork are the one way that he can bring together and showcase his three states of being: manic, depressive, and stable; and invite the audience to get to know him more deeply than he had realized possible.

The performance exits the audience through the artist’s working studio and a small gallery of selected paintings.  The paintings are cleverly captioned and displayed in a way that lacks the frills and cleanliness of a typical art gallery, but in doing so invites audiences into the warmth and humanity that the artist exudes.  The exhibit contains works like “The Factory” which showcases a cow-like-figure who is “just as lost as you are about who she is” and “Therapy” which contains illegible markings and symbols as the artist tries to “decipher his learnings from a therapy session.”

Part comedy routine, part melodrama, part art exhibition, 300 Paintings is a must catch this season. It will charm you, move you, and encourage you to question the status quo and leap into the beautiful abyss of the unexpected.

 

300 PAINTINGS – created and performed by Sam Kissajukian

Scenic and lighting specialist, Oona Curley; production stage manager, Esti Bernstein; Press Representative, The Press Room; production manager, Rebecca Schaffer; interim general manager, Moogie Brooks.  Presented by the Vineyard Theatre: Sarah Stern & Douglas Aibel, artistic directors; 108 East 15th Street, New York. Through December 15th; 80 minutes not intermission. https://vineyardtheatre.org/shows/300-paintings

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

When the doors open the audience enters onto a darkened stage. A woman sits on a chair facing away from the audience. She is watching, projected on a screen, the story of Agamemnon and his wife Clytemnestra told in news clips, films. It unfolds in jumps quick flashes. Behind the screen hangs a clothesline full of clothes. The clothes are hanging on hangers. Hanging like bodies. Clothes signifying the thousands of humans who are displaced by war. Families who walk out of their country into others to seek safety and a new life. This is their story and ours, the story of we humans who choose war repeatedly. Choose the battle of greed for power, land, and control over those who live under our power.

Rafika Chawishe makes her US debut at La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club with her heartbreaking 60-minute re-telling of Aeschylus’ “Agamemnon” entitled Agamemnon The Circle of Blood. This is a multimedia telling with actual film footage and reenactments of past wars and the wars going on today. Images of refugee camps today and young children laughing and chasing after the drones that are filming them. Children living in squalor because their families had to leave their homes or be killed. The video of those sweet children chasing after the drone is heart-wrenching.

Chawishe did not create this from reading about it. She was there. Working at the border of Greece helping families crossover. Many children. Children crossing alone, put on this journey by their parents in hopes that they will live and thrive. I think of the Kinder transport created to get children out of Nazi Germany and Poland. Children prosecuted for no reason but their religion. Here children are prosecuted for no reason but their nationality.

Chawishe combines the film footage with monologues of those who have made it over. One, a woman in a blood-stained shirt being told that she will have to fill out papers and then wait two years to find out if she can remain in the country or be sent back. While waiting, she cannot work or get a job, find proper housing, or start a life of any kind. They must wait TWO YEARS in a tent in a refugee camp to find out if they can start life over again or not. The paperwork, the hoops to jump through, are daunting and insurmountable.

And Chawishe arrives to us as Clytemnestra the wife of Agamemnon. Clytemnestra will herself be soaked in blood. In the blood of her husband murdered by Agamemnon’s cousin/her lover, Aegisthus. Murdered to avenge the murder of Clytemnestra’s daughter Iphigenia whom Agamemnon sacrificed to the goddess Artemis to appease her for favorable winds. After the sacrifice Artemis allows the winds to blow and thus Agamemnon’s fleet sets sail to conquer Troy. Clytemnestra is a woman witnessing and living the insanity of it all. To avenge one murder with another debases all involved. The question to ask is are all of us at the mercy of hatred? Hate and revenge? Well, if our Gods require sacrifices then so shall we.
The theater is filled with the sounds of helicopters flying overhead and bombs exploding. All of it is so loud the floor rumbles and the seats shake. This is the reality of living in a war zone.

Chawishe says this production is her way of protesting. Protesting the wars and the treatment of the refugees seeking safety. She creates precise awareness for the viewer to see what needs to be protested. The harsh treatment of the refugees and the ridiculous amount of paperwork that is so complicated that you need a translator for it.

Agamemnon: The Circle of Blood is a powerful 60 minutes. You won’t go away untouched.

Agamemnon: The Circle of Blood World Premiere Concept, direction, and performance by Rafika Chawishe Writer : Aeschylus , Yiannis Ritsos ( Agamemnon )

LaMama The Downstairs
66 East 4th Street, basement level
New York, NY 10003

Through November 24 – Tickets: Adults: $30, Students/Seniors: $25, First 10 tickets are $10 (limit 2 per person) Ticket prices are inclusive of all fees.

Late seating is not permitted for this performance.

This performance is in English, Greek, and Arabic (English subtitles).

title.rendered: Lucidity: A World Premiere by On Site Opera

content.rendered:
Lucidity: A World Premiere by On Site Opera

By Edward Kliszus

On Site Opera and Seattle Opera’s co-production of Lucidity: A World Premiere by On Site Opera, offered an awe-inspiring and transformative journey into the profound connections between memory, music, and science. Performed at the Abrons Arts Center, this emotionally stirring production captivated audiences. By exploring how music connects fragmented memories and serves as a source of healing, Lucidity provided a deeply personal experience that lingered long after the final curtain fell.

With its innovative staging and emotionally resonant themes, Lucidity, a profoundly moving musical work—emphasizes the relationship between music and memory. This opera is an artistic achievement and a brilliant showcase of music’s enduring connection to the human experience.

The Power of Music and Memory in Lucidity’s Narrative

At the heart of Lucidity is the story of Lili, portrayed by the legendary Lucy Shelton. Lili, a former soprano, composer, and professor of music, struggles with early dementia. Once a celebrated figure in the music world, she now finds her memories slipping away. Meanwhile, her son Dante, played by the heartfelt Eric McKeever, sacrifices his career as a pianist to care for her, though he regrets leaving music behind. Together, they represent the bittersweet dynamics of caregiving and the enduring bond between parent and child.

Additionally, Dr. Klugman, portrayed by Blythe Gaissert, adds an intellectual layer to the story. Once Lili’s student at the conservatory, Dr. Klugman shifted her career toward science. Frustrated by her inability to complete her book on music therapy, she grapples with whether music’s essence can be measured scientifically or only experienced emotionally.

Finally, Sunny, played by the radiant Cristina Maria Castro, bridges these worlds as a clarinetist and music therapist. Tasked with working with Lili, Sunny’s artistry becomes a critical turning point for the characters. Her work inspires Dr. Klugman to realize that music and science are interconnected. This revelation allows Dr. Klugman to move forward with her book, solidifying music’s dual role as art and therapy.

Eric McKeever Baritone. Photo courtesy of ericmckeeverbaritone.com. Lucy Shelton, Soprano. Photo by Karjaka Studios

Innovative Staging and Music’s Role in Lucidity

Immersive Staging Highlights Music and Memory

Under Sarah Meyer’s brilliant direction, Lucidity immersed its audience in the story’s emotional depths. The audience was seated on risers behind the stage, giving them a unique perspective of the performers on the main stage, the balcony, and even among the theater seats. This dynamic staging reflected Lili’s memories’ fluid and fragmented nature, directly connecting the audience to her journey.

The orchestra, conducted masterfully by Geoffrey McDonald, was placed in the theater pit at the heart of the staging, symbolizing music’s central role in the narrative. The orchestra’s literal placement underscored its symbolic importance as the pulse of Lili’s story, connecting her memories and identity to the present.

Music and Memory: The Emotional Core of Lucidity

Laura Kaminsky’s stunning score exemplified music’s duality as an emotional and scientific force. The tension between dissonance and harmony paralleled the characters’ internal conflicts. The emotional apex came when Lili performed Schubert’s Shepherd on the Rock, her soprano voice soaring with clarity and passion. This powerful moment demonstrated music’s unparalleled ability to unlock memory and emotion.

Complementing Kaminsky’s exceptional music is David Cote’s poetic and evocative libretto, which effortlessly ties together loss, healing, and memory themes. Moreover, Cote’s text authentically gives the characters a voice that resonates deeply with audiences through its thoughtful and emotional dialogue. The lyrics, meanwhile, balance Dr. Klugman’s scientific inquiry with Lili’s vulnerability and Sunny’s hopeful resilience. Together, Cote’s libretto and Kaminsky’s music create a seamless tapestry, elevating Lucidity into an extraordinary modern opera experience.

The orchestra, featuring members of the American Modern Ensemble, brought Kaminsky’s composition to life with remarkable virtuosity. Yasmina Speigelberg’s clarinet embodied the healing power of music therapy, serving as an emotional guide throughout the story. Meanwhile, Kyle Walker’s piano added warmth and depth, particularly during therapy sessions involving Lili, Dante, Sunny, and Dr. Klugman.

Supporting musicians, including Dave Eggar (cello), Nikita Mozorov (violin), and Brandon Williams (percussion), added texture and nuance to the narrative. Under McDonald’s guidance, they created a musical tapestry that deepened the audience’s connection to the characters.

L-R Cristina Maria Castro, Soprano. Photo by Sub/Urban Photography. Blythe Gaissert, Mezzo Soprano. Courtesy blythegaissert.com

A Cast That Brings Music and Memory to Life

Lucy Shelton Shines as Lili

The legendary Lucy Shelton gave an unforgettable performance as Lili. Her fragile and powerful soprano voice captured the complexities of her character—a woman who struggles to retain her identity through the fog of dementia. Shelton’s portrayal of Lili as a towering musical figure and a vulnerable individual was profoundly moving.

Eric McKeever and Cristina Maria Castro Deliver Emotional Performances

Eric McKeever brought depth and humanity to his portrayal of Dante, balancing regret and love as he cared for his mother. His heart-wrenching duets with Shelton illustrated the emotional intricacies of their relationship.

Meanwhile, Cristina Maria Castro dazzled as Sunny. Her ethereal soprano voice and emotional range brought her character to life, making her a beacon of hope within the story. Castro’s musical artistry, paired with Speigelberg’s clarinet, created some of the production’s most transcendent moments.

Blythe Gaissert’s Dr. Klugman Provides Depth

Blythe Gaissert infused Dr. Klugman with intellectual gravitas and emotional vulnerability. Her mezzo-soprano lines reflected her internal struggle between science and emotion. Ultimately, her character’s realization that “music is science” provided an operatic, cathartic, and satisfying resolution.

Laura Kaminsky, Composer. Photo by Rebecca Allan. David Cote, Librettist. Photo courtesy davidcote.com

Visual and Technical Elements Enhance Lucidity’s Themes

Lighting and Costumes Highlight Emotional Depth

Lighting transitions between shadow and illumination mirrored the shifting clarity of Lili’s mind. Additionally, Elizabeth Clark’s costume design underscored each character’s development. For example, Lili’s wardrobe evolved from structured to subdued as her memories faded, while Sunny’s bright and professional attire highlighted her optimism.

Props Anchor Music and Memory in Lucidity

The piano in Lili’s apartment served as a central prop, connecting characters to their pasts. Other elements, such as Lili’s musical compositions scattered across the set, symbolized the fragments of her memory and creativity.

The Triumphant Resolution of Music and Memory

Ultimately, Lucidity’s resolution was both intellectually satisfying and emotionally resonant. Dr. Klugman’s realization that music and science are inherently connected affirmed the opera’s central theme: music’s ability to heal and connect is both measurable and deeply personal. As Dr. Klugman moved forward with her book, her journey mirrored the audience’s renewed understanding of music’s transformative power.

On Site Opera troupe standing for final bows in Lucidity. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Final Thoughts: A Must-See Celebration of Music and Memory

On-Site Opera and Seattle Opera’s Lucidity is an exceptional example of opera’s ability to illuminate life’s most complex truths. Through its exploration of memory, music, and science, this production inspires a renewed appreciation for the resilience of the human spirit. For anyone seeking an opera that challenges, uplifts, and transforms, Lucidity is a must-see.

title.rendered: Karen Ackers’ “Feels Like Home” at Birdland

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

“Home is where we learn who we are… and also where we are scarred for life,” Karen Akers joked to her warm audience at Birdland, encapsulating the endearing mix of sentimentality and humor that ran through her show, “Feels Like Home.” The evening of songs felt like a homecoming in many ways for Akers, who welcomed the crowd to her “biannual one night stand” at the famed jazz locale. 

The show was imbued with the rosiness of looking back on one’s past. For Akers, that included hearkening back to her Broadway years with ballads from Les Misérables and Chess, mixed in with nostalgic nods to the Carpenters and Crosby, Still, Nash and Young. Accompanied sparsely by her music director Alex Rybeck on piano and Tom Hubbard on the upright bass, Akers hid nothing. The show was intimate and raw, allowing for moments of wobbliness in an otherwise masterful performance. 

Anytime we return home, we are bound to find things both familiar and strange, changed by the passing of time. For an audience that has known Akers since she debuted on Broadway in 1982 as Luisa Contini in Nine, some may be surprised to hear how her voice has matured over time. Rather than attempting to obscure potential weak points, Akers played to her strengths. With masterful vocal control and an innate understanding of dramatic tension, Akers showcased her decades of artistic experience. Her signature alto crooning wrapped gently around every lyric, giving a delicate quality to songs like Randy Newman’s “Feels Like Home” and Carly Simon’s “The Boys in the Trees.” Akers’ performance was well suited to the intimate setting of Birdland, seductively begging the audience to lean in and listen to a fresh interpretation of beloved songs.

Akers is no stranger to the cabaret stage, and her comfort with crowd banter showed it. She knew when to soothe her listeners with sentiment, such as when she quoted Tennessee Williams as saying, “I don’t regard a home as a place… I think of a home as being a thing that two people have between them in which each can…well, nest.” She knew when to crack a joke, often with a girlish smile as though she was getting away with something. Akers’ slyness allowed her to hit comedic moments well. In her rendition of Sondheim’s “I Never Do Anything Twice,” Akers invited her audience to indulge in a juvenile sense of mischief with her, clutching a hand to her neck as though scandalized by her own devilishness. She pulled off a charming coyness that kept you transfixed for the entirety of the show. 

In a time of great political uncertainty and defeatism, Akers brought a refreshing feeling of common humanity to her show. Her rendition of “Anthem” from Chess was quietly moving as she put all her power behind the lyric, “I cross over borders, but I’m still there now.” Her themes of home and belonging soon morphed into larger sentiments about the country and our connection to it. In another number, she acknowledged feelings of political frustration, singing “When I was young / elections had their charms / but that’s been wearing kind of thin.” Towards the end of the night, she told the story of how she almost turned down her first invitation to sing at the White House. This was while President Ronald Reagan was in office, and she had not voted for him. Her friend convinced her to take the gig by saying, “It’s not his house. It’s ours.” For those who may be struggling with their relationship to home, Akers provided a space that was both nostalgic and unsettled, allowing everyone to consider how we can truly find a place to call our own. Perhaps, it is not a place we are seeking at all, but as Tennessee Williams and Karen Akers demonstrate, a person we can connect to, in a time we need them most.

FEELS LIKE HOME was a one-night show performed by Karen Akers at BIRDLAND JAZZ CLUB on Monday, November 18 with musical director Alex Rybeck on piano and Tom Hubbard on bass.

content.rendered:
by Margret Echeverria

In an effort to keep me out of trouble, my parents recruited my aunt to make a Midwest “Regular” Baptist out of me.  The Praise The Lord – PTL – Network  was frowned-upon viewing in my house because those people proselytized a “Prosperity Gospel” that was irregular, to say the least.  But I was precocious, so I would sneak-watch the PTL Network as well as Dr. Ruth Westheimer any chance I got.  Last night, I found myself in an audience loaded with Gen X’ers, who did the same, all eager to witness the new Broadway musical TAMMY FAYE at the Palace Theatre directed by Rupert Goold, featuring music by Elton John.  This show was made for us — those of us who loved Tammy Faye because she was a “real” Christian.  It is not made for people delighting in the media feast on the spoils of Heritage USA wanting to leave a good person in a nest of rattle snakes.

Katie Brayben is Tammy Faye in this production and unlike Faye herself, Brayben has an incredible set of pipes.  Tammy Faye was born and raised as Pentecostal in Minnesota, just a few miles from where I grew up, so I found the American Southern drawl that occasionally snuck into Brayben’s speech to be misplaced, but I was able to forgive this common mistake by British performers because Brayben fully embodies my icon in every movement of her body and facial expression combined with a perfect imitation of the rhythm of Tammy Faye’s speech making the very essence of Tammy Faye consistently present throughout the show.  I was crying just a few minutes in for how much I miss the comfort of Tammy Faye’s perfect agape love.

Elton John’s music, Katrina Lindsay’s shoulder padded costumes and Bunny Christie‘s hilarious game show on ‘roids scenic designs brilliantly conjure the oily plastic ‘80’s making us nostalgic for the days when the most evil thing in the world was Ronald Reagan and the air always smelled like synthetic perfumes.  Christian Borle gives Jim Bakker a very fun physical comedy element that is not part of Bakker’s real-life persona, but I thought this was a clever way to symbolize what is real in Bakker: He is such an awkward Minnesota Lake Trout dropped into the Red Sea of an evangelist’s existence where Jonah’s whale lies in wait.  Historically, Bakker is harder to forgive because he is a misogynist keeping Tammy Faye blind to the financial sorcery he makes reasoning that she, as a woman, cannot be useful in such matters.  Mark Evans, I must say, is is adorable and true to Billy Graham who many remember played from the heart, however misguided it may have been.  But fundamental to the fall of the well-intentioned Bakkers are the false profits Jimmy Swaggart (Ian Lassiter), Jerry Falwell (Michael Cerveris) and Pat Robertson (Andy Taylor).  Michael Cerveris, painted Falwell as so absurd with subtle comic insight mirroring the

Michael Cerveris, Christian Borle and Katie Brayben in TAMMY FAYE. Photo by Matthew Murphy.

monster that the man truly was; a necessary reflection, I think, to cool the fires of our rage.  Falwell’s cloak of anti-Christ could not hide his dagger from the wisdom of Tammy Faye’s heavily mascaraed vision.  Her insistence on loving everyone withered Falwell’s legacy when she interviewed Steve Pieters (Charl Brown) on the PTL Network and encouraged us to love and hug our HIV positive brothers and sisters in Christ.  This triumphant moment on stage is as real as a musical portrait of a world altering moment can get.  Kleenex, please.

Tammy Faye taught us that love wins every time.  If I hadn’t been wearing tube mascara, brought to market after Tammy Faye’s death, it would have been running down my cheeks by the end of this show.  We need to insert as much love as the world can take into these modern times and Tammy Faye reminds us to not give up “until Heaven.”  See this show and get nourished by a little slice of life lived by a generous departed soul and maybe you, too, will find strength to make a difference.

TAMMY FAYE Directed by Rupert Goold, Book by James Graham, Lyrics by Jake Shears (of the Scissor Sisters, People!!), Music by Elton John.

WITH Katie Brayben (Tammy Faye Bakker), Christian Borle (Jim Bakker), Michael Cerveris (Jerry Falwell), Autumn Hurlbert (Tammy Faye Bakker Alternate), Nick Bailey (Paul Crouch), Charl Brown (Steve Pieters), Mark Evans (Billy Graham, Larry Flynt, Charles Shepard), Allison Guinn (Jan Crouch), Ian Lassiter (Jimmy Swaggart, Ronald Reagan, Archbishop of Canterbury), Raymond J. Lee (John Fletcher), Max Gordon Moore (Proctologist, Marvin Gorman, Thomas S. Monson), Alana Pollard (Jessica Hahn), and Andy Taylor (Pat Robertson, Ted Turner, Pope John Paul II), as well as Ensemble actors Amanda Clement, Michael Di Liberto, Jonathan Duvelson, Lily Kaufmann, Denis Lambert, Elliott Mattox, Brittany Nicholas, Keven Quillon, Aveena Sawyer, Allysa Shorte, TJ Tapp, Daniel Torres, and Dana Wilton

Scenic design by Bunny Christie, costume design by Katrina Lindsay, lighting design by Neil Austin, video design by Finn Ross, and sound design by Nick Lidster for Autograph, orchestrations by Mark Dickman and Tom Deering, and music supervision, arrangements, and additional music by Tom Deering.

Through March 30, 2025 at The Palace Theatre, 160 West 47th Street, NYC.  Get tickets here.

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

To start off with, I’m not a laugher, a smiler, but not a laugher (could be a control thing as you have to tickle my brain as much as my funny bone), so suffice it to say, I laughed.

Beginning with the mantra, “If you don’t bring forth what is within you, it will kill you,” Blaire Postman brings it all forth in her tightly clipped personal reveal of a show entitled Lady ADHD. She pointedly walks her audience through the unreliable amount of noise and tornado-like whirling that happens inside her brain and the paths it pulls her body down. If you’ve ever been curious about such a trip, you can take this safely guided tour with her as your guide without ever having to leave the farm.

Maybe you have ADHD or a smidgen thereof, you may live with someone who does (even though they wont admit it), or it’s ever crossed your mind (about you or them), Ms. Postman’s show is a delightful reveal down a tightly structured way of looking at the world. And to illuminate this hallway without exits she has placed on the stage six red sequined covered flipcharts that take the audience, accompanied by illustrations, into the in-depth history of half-time Super Bowl shows (you’ll know more about Al Hirt and Carol Channing than you did before), Thiscatischunky Facebook group (and its dirivitives), the book The Giving Tree and its writer Shel Silverstein, the First Amendment (how it’s used as both a sheild and a sword), and School House Rock. She then ties them all up in their surprising interconnectedness at the end. A phenominal feat, a revealing show, and a gifted performer.

Blaire does talk about during the course of the show, the needed acceptance of this neurodiversity and what people with this viewpoint bring to the world: their focusness, their dogged determination to see something to the end, and their take on how everthing, in the big picture of things, is tied together in some way if we only look hard enough. This type of person, she laments, is apt to be the one to find the cure for cancer. It takes this incredible type of focus to boldly go where no one has gone before.

—–

Blaire Postman is Lady ADHD, playing for only a short time (December 12-15, 2024) at the downstairs Huron Club at Soho Rep.

Runtime 65 minutes.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“Thou shouldst not have been old till thou hadst been wise.”

Let me start by saying that as a fervent theater lover, you should go and see this production of King Lear just because Kenneth Branagh did it. He, more than almost anyone else I can think of, has brought Shakespeare’s relevance to us groundings in the many plays and films, penned by Shakespeare, that he has touched. Those efforts, individually and cumulatively, are worth our attention as they build upon each other and make this present work all the more approachable, succinct, and relevant. If his work has ever enamored you, what you can glean from this offering, and his portrayal of Lear, is an understanding of the character’s journey and an application of universal themes of youth, trust, power, and love that never seem to wain.

I will also add that I don’t completely agree with all of his choices (I do applaud the double casting of Cordelia and the Fool) but absolutely understand the reasoning behind why he made the choices he did. That clarity inspires and revitalizes my thinking and ultimate understanding of the play. Bravo! to that.

I don’t think I need to tell you the story of King Lear, but if you want, here is a fun synopsis.

A major focus of this production is the youth that Lear is relinquishing his stature, rule, and kingdom to, raising them up as he realizes his time is drawing nigh and he wants to go out on top, a paragon of leadership, honored and loved. Branagh has cast the production full of up-and-coming graduates of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) where he was past president (and a graduate in his youth) and, though I may not side with that choice, I understand how its execution adds to one of the themes of what Lear is about, when is the right time to step aside, when do you let the reigns go? They all play their parts well (a couple of standouts Jessica Revell as Cordelia and the Fool, Doug Colling as Edgar) and I could say good things about each one. Still, I can’t help but feel that this choice of flooding the cast with youth does take away from the play’s gravity at times as immortality accompanies youth like a henna tattoo, temporary, but hard to get off and appearing permanent. Lear is anything but permanent and flux and change are a constant theme.

Through the years Lear has been approached in many ways in trying to understand and justify his actions of demanding the vocalizations of love from his daughters before divvying up his land to the three of them. Some played it that he was already addled in the head, some played the egocentric king demanding loyalty that was only in his mind and forces a justification, and others saw him as a buffoon. Mr. Branagh plays him as conscious of what he is doing, confident in his choices, and utterly surprised by their repercussions. It still doesn’t answer the question for me completely, but I also have to realize I may never get an answer as it is one of the first questions addressed at every production’s table read.

This is a play full of sound and fury, signifying everything and clips along coming in at two hours without an intermission (in many productions the first act ends at the two-hour mark). This pacing keeps the through-lines of the story clipping along, more like a trot, and doesn’t give the audience too much time to think as we need to keep vigilant as things happen one right after the other. No petty pace here. What you have is a well-told story, played by an excellent cast, directed and staged with a sharpness and alacrity that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

—–

King Lear by William Shakespeare, Co-Directed by Rob Ashford, Kenneth Branagh, and Lucy Skilbeck.

With Mara Allen (Curan), Deborah Alli (Goneril), Raymond Anum (Burgundy), Saffron Coomber (Regan), Kenneth Branagh (King Lear), Doug Colling (Edgar), Stefan Brennan-Healy (France), Eleanor De Rohan (Kent), Chloe Fenwick‐Brown (Oswald), Joseph Kloska (Gloucester), Dylan Corbett-Bader  (Edmund), Hughie O’Donnell (Cornwall), Caleb Obediah (Albany), and Jessica Revell (Cordelia/The Fool).

Creative team: Jon Bausor (set and costume designer),  (co-director), Aletta Collins (choreographer), Nina Dunn (projection designer), Paul Keogan (lighting designer), Ben and Max Ringham (sound designers and composers), and Bret Yount (fight director).

Through December 15.  Tickets are available at www.theshed.org

Guests under 30 years old may purchase up to two tickets at the front of the theater at $25 each.

content.rendered:
Carmina Burana and More by the Oratorio Society of New York

by Edward Kliszus

The Oratorio Society of New York opened its 2024-25 season with a dynamic concert featuring Carl Orff’s Carmina Burana at Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium/Perelman Stage. As the full house settled into the grand hall, attendees eagerly browsed superb program books filled with notes on the music, artists, and song texts in both German and Latin, with English translations.

Billboard is announcing the premiere of Carl Orff’s Carmina Burana in Valencia, Spain, with Luis Ximénez Caballero conducting the Municipal Orchestra of Valencia (1960). Laurieximenez, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

An Evening of Timeless Music by the Oratorio Society of New York

Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium echoed with timeless music as the Oratorio Society of New York (OSNY) began its season with an unforgettable performance. Conducted by David Rosenmeyer, the concert featured pianists Amir Farid and Blair McMillen, alongside the Oratorio Society chorus, a percussion ensemble, and the Choristers of the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. Together, they created an ensemble supercharged with talent and power. The program also included the New York premiere of Oliver Caplan’s “Cloud Anthem,” Libby Larsen’s “Invitation to Music,” two songs by Franz Schubert, and selections from Brahms’ Liebeslieder, Op. 42.

World-Class Soloists Shine in Carmina Burana and More

The Oratorio Society welcomed soprano Eva Rae Martinez, tenor John Riesen, and baritone John Brancy as soloists. They brought inspiration, emotion, and musical mastery to the season’s opening. Notably, Martinez and Riesen made their Carnegie Hall debuts, adding a particular highlight to the evening.

Johannes Brahms: A Touching Performance of Liebeslieder, Op. 42

The ensemble delivered a stunning rendition of Brahms’ Liebeslieder selections. They captured the interplay of longing and restraint that defines Brahms’ work.  Notably, “Rede, Mädchen, allzu liebes” resounded with gentle, earnest appeal, while “Am Gesteine rauscht die Flut” conveyed timeless beauty. Likewise, “Am Donaustrande” highlights Brahms’ melodic depth. Next, the choir performed “O wie sanft die Quelle” with tenderness, evoking the softness of spring, while “Nein, es ist nicht auszukommen” added playful energy. They concluded with “Schlosser auf, und mache Schlösser,” performed with vigor, capturing Brahms’ emotional intensity.

Through a polished performance, the Oratorio Society of New York allowed the audience to appreciate the elegance of Brahms’ Liebeslieder, creating a memorable tribute to his genius.

The Fellinger family with Johannes Brahms (1896) Public Domain

Libby Larsen: A Heartfelt Invitation to Music

Libby Larsen’s Invitation to Music is a tonal work with a dash of dissonance that hints at irony. The Oratorio Society’s performance captured the essence and subtle beauty of Larsen’s composition with skill and emotion.

Larsen composed Invitation to Music to evoke the experience of deep listening, a theme she discussed with Bob Phibbs, the original commissioner. Setting it to Elizabeth Bishop’s poem “Sonnet,” which speaks to simplicity and depth, Larsen’s work reflects music’s universal kindness. The Oratorio Society conveyed this “gentle invitation” with a polished, heartfelt interpretation that drew the audience into a reflective, healing space. Their performance honored Larsen’s vision and celebrated the kindness and beauty music offers to all its “humble partakers.”

Oliver Caplan: Cloud Anthem – A Celebration of Unity and Diversity

The Oratorio Society’s rendition of Oliver Caplan’s Cloud Anthem was powerful and moving. Rooted in the theme of unity through diversity, Cloud Anthem celebrates community, using music to symbolize America’s strength in diversity.

Inspired by Richard Blanco’s poem, Caplan designed Cloud Anthem to convey the power of unity within diversity. Just as different pieces of fabric can form a beautiful quilt, Caplan’s composition combines musical themes of harmony, resilience, and unity. The choir’s voices blended seamlessly, reinforcing that individual identities can coexist harmoniously.

The Oratorio Society’s skillful performance emphasized Cloud Anthem‘s message, showing how music can bridge differences and inspire togetherness. This performance beautifully embodied Caplan’s vision of community as an art form, leaving the audience moved and inspired.

Franz Schubert by Wilhelm August Rieder 1875. Public Domain

Franz Schubert: Der Tanz, D. 826, and Lebenslust, D. 609 – Celebrating Joy and Community

Franz Schubert’s Der Tanz and Lebenslust radiate joy and human connection through music. Both pieces reflect Schubert’s ability to create buoyant melodies with a warm, communal spirit.

The performance of Der Tanz was lively and spirited, with brisk tempos and playful rhythms that conveyed Schubert’s lyrical charm. The choir’s crisp articulation highlighted the festive energy of the piece, creating a sense of celebration. In Lebenslust, the ensemble embraced warmth and optimism, conveying companionship’s joy. The Oratorio Society captured the camaraderie Schubert intended, delivering the piece with finesse, combining technical skill and emotional warmth.

Carl Orff: Carmina Burana – A Masterpiece of Power and Emotion

Under the expert direction of David Rosenmeyer, the Oratorio Society of New York delivered an electrifying performance of Carl Orff’s Carmina Burana at Carnegie Hall. Known for its intense themes of fate, love, and revelry, Carmina Burana explores the power of choral and orchestral music.

From the thunderous opening of “O Fortuna,” the choir commanded the stage, immersing the audience in Orff’s world with striking dramatic effect. The Oratorio Society demonstrated strength and sensitivity, skillfully navigating Orff’s score’s complex dynamics and rhythms. Rosenmeyer’s leadership enabled the ensemble to express the emotions that define Carmina Burana, capturing the essence of fate and human passion.

The Three Vocal Soloists in Carmina Burana

Soprano Eva Rae Martinez, tenor John Riesen, and baritone John Brancy showcased extraordinary vocal artistry in their solos. Martinez’s crystalline voice brought purity and expressiveness to “In Trutina,” imbuing it with vulnerability and grace. Riesen infused “Olim lacus colueram” with energy and precision, demonstrating agility and dramatic power. Brancy’s rich baritone brought depth and humor to “Ego sum abbas,” capturing the audience with his magnetic stage presence.

L-R John Brancy, Baritone. Photo by Gerard Collet. John Riesen, Tenor. Courtesy insagram.com:johnriesen. Eva Martinez, Soprano. Courtesy insagram.com:evamartinez

Powerful Instrumental Accompaniment for Orff’s Vision

The skilled pianists Amir Farid and Blair McMillen and the Oratorio Society’s percussionists created a vivid soundscape that amplified Orff’s decisive score. Moreover, the acoustics of Carnegie Hall further enriched the performance, allowing each beat and vocal nuance to resonate fully.

An Unforgettable Evening with the Oratorio Society of New York

The Oratorio Society of New York, led by the talented David Rosenmeyer, along with Martinez, Riesen, Brancy, and the exceptional instrumental ensemble, delivered a performance of Carmina Burana that left a lasting impression. This powerful celebration of Orff’s masterpiece and other timeless works captivated the audience with musical excellence and emotional depth. After extended ovations, attendees departed Carnegie Hall, moved and exhilarated by a night of artistic command that will not soon be forgotten.

Don’t miss this season’s upcoming performances by the Oratorio Society of New York. For information and tickets, click HERE.

Oratorio Society of New York standing to extended ovations in Carnegie Hall. Photo by Edward Kliszus
