content.rendered:
By David Walters

Playwright Michael Quinn has penned a two-handed Gen Z angst-ridden dramady about trying to figure out who you are called Get It Together. It’s an age-old question that never seems to get answered no matter the Gen.

What he successfully created in his writing was a clear differentiation between the two characters, snuggly getting into the shoes of each and presenting their specific non-sequitured gender points of view. Not an easy task.

The strikingly raw but amateurish poems he pens for Mary (played with an edgy innocence by Hadley Durkee), his female character, are spot on, revealing her true self in their vulnerability, opening her up to the tragedy of a relationship that can only work in the recesses of her mind. “Your eyes are blue like candy and your body is soft with womb.”

Her emotionally meandering male foil, Harold (Joseph Basquill, lost to the meaning of self-aware), is ruled by his other head, and in meeting Mary, stops for a moment in his stumbling through life seeking to find a place called home. Mary gives him that pause, but he has no idea what to do with it.

In Get It Together Mary and Harold are back home from college during a break and end up connecting at a party. Mary is an artsy type and Harold is into computers. She has had a crush on Harold for some time since they spent hours talking at a previous party. Harold brings her up to the bedroom of the sister of a friend of his to have sex. Mary reminds him about their previous conversation (which he doesn’t remember) and his current long-time on-again-off-again girlfriend whom he constantly cheats on. They end up talking about their past, their present, and what their futures may be in a push-me-pull-you way that keeps them figuratively circling round the bed and its ultimate purpose. Harold is kept off balance by Mary during this tango as she actually listens to him, as he states no one previously had. They have sex.

Second act, it’s two years later and Harold surreptitiously shows up at a party that Mary is hosting claiming he didn’t know it was her apartment. He is no longer attached and his constant fear of being alone has kept Mary in his mind. She is angered because she felt that she had finally purged him from her being and his presence belies that false belief. They recognize that they are still drawn to each other, “And who will understand me, if not you?,” but are afraid to admit that is about all there probably is.

Sean Penn described his relationship with Madonna as a tremendous first date, but that was all there was. (They were together for four years; you can’t say they didn’t try.)

There’s too much repetition of arguments that seem to go on for much longer than they should, the ending in a freeze frame is incongruous with the rest of the play, we understand why he is attracted to her, but not so much the other way round as he doesn’t seem to have any redeeming values. And despite all of this there is something of value in this production.

Both actors, Hadley Durkee and Joseph Basquill, are conscious of the incongruities of their characters and work very hard to establish a depth of connection, which they do, and that makes the play worth watching as they are pulled along by something that is completely wrong for them, but do it anyway, pulled by something deeper within that overrules the logic of the brain.

The writing of these Gen Z characters is both compelling and put-offish, successful in that application as it reflects the inner emotional mess of the characters and makes for a compelling story.

There’s some good stuff here, worthy of a look, and worthy to keep tabs on what is coming next from the playwright’s laptop.

—–

Get It Together is performing at the downstairs Flea Theater starring Hadley Durkee and Joseph Basquill, produced by Andie Lerner, and written and directed by playwright Michael Quinn.

The production features scenic and prop design by Lily Guerin, lighting design by Kristen Paige, sound design by Julianne Mason, and costumes by Lisa Zinni.
Tickets can be purchased here.

title.rendered: A WONDERFUL WORLD: THE LOUIS ARMSTRONG MUSICAL

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

“Jazz is about the choices you make between the notes,” Louis Armstrong says to the rehearsal pianist at the beginning of the show, “and you make those choices based on the heart.”  A Wonderful World packs a lot of heart between each of its iconic tunes as it tells us the story of one of jazz’s most influential trumpeters.

Spanning his decades-long career, we start with a young Armstrong in New Orleans, just beginning his journey of spreading jazz and happiness to those around him.  Full of love, the story follows Armstrong through his four wives, all of whom influenced him in a variety of ways.  While Satchmo smiles throughout the piece, it doesn’t take long for the Jim Crow South to cast a shadow on his demeanor and road bumps along his path.  Nevertheless, Armstrong persists with the help of his own determination and strong women at this side.  His path takes him from Chicago to Hollywood, to New York City, as he runs to escape his standing as a black man in America all while becoming one of the most beloved musicians of the century.

A Wonderful World, conceived by Andrew Delaplaine and director, Christopher Renshaw with a book by Aurin Squire contains all of the joy and positivity of Louis Armstrong himself, while floating along the undercurrent of racism and segregation in America.  It’s about a man who loved his country enough to want to change the way that people saw it, who struggled to overcome the obstacle of racism, and who eventually began to speak out, almost ending his career for doing so.

James Monre Iglehart and the company in A Wonderful World: The Louis Armstrong Musical; photo by Jeremy Daniel

James Monroe Iglehart absolutely charms as Louis Armstrong, smiling from ear to ear and crooning with joy, juxtaposed with the difficult decisions, broken hearts, and injustices that Armstrong endured.  Your eyes are drawn to him and yet, if you closed them, you’d imagine it was the trumpeter himself you were listening to on the stage.  

Monroe is surrounded by a fierce ensemble of women playing Armstrong’s four wives: Dionne Figgins (Daisy Parker), Jennie Harney-Fleming (Lil Hardin), Kim Exum (Alpha Smith), and Darlesia Cearcy (Lucille Wilson).  Each of these women helped to lift the talented musician to stardom and gave him something for the journey: fight, control, fun, and stability.  

The rest of the ensemble lights up the stage with Rickey Tripp’s inspired choreography, transporting us from New Orleans jazz clubs of the 1910s to the Cotton Club of NYC in the 40s and beyond.

The design for the production is stellar.  Adam Koch and Steven Royal’s scenic and video design heighten each environment, highlighting Armstrong’s love of touring (and running away) with oversized trunks and suitcases bookending the performing space, and a large proscenium that transforms from elevated railway line to bandstand and more.   Toni-Leslie James’ costumes stun as they glitter and gleam across the stage in Cory Pattak’s lighting, and Kai Harada’s sound design creates a true 360 experience in the theater as rattles of train cars and other city sounds seem to echo across the orchestra.

As a black man living in Jim Crow, it’s inspiring to see how Louis Armstrong smiled through it all, but also to be able to understand the toll that came along with it.   A Wonderful World is an important story, a hopeful story with a sunny disposition, a story that believes in the possibility of change and in seeing the beauty in the world and trying to build a better one – with music and with love.

 

A WONDERFUL WORLD –  book by Aurin Squire; conceived by Andrew Delaplaine and Christopher Renshaw

Directed by Christopher Renshaw; co-direction by James Monroe Iglehart & Christina Sajous; music supervisions, vocal and incidental musical arrangements and additional orchestrations by Daryl Waters; orchestrations and arrangements by Branford Marsalis; choreography and musical staging by Rickey Tripp.

FEATURING: James Monroe Iglehart; Darlesia Cearcy; Kim Exum; Dionne Figgins; Jennie Harney-Fleming; Trista Dollison; Dewitt Fleming Jr.; Jason Forbach; Gavin Gregory; James T. Lane; Jimmy Smagula; Brandon Louis Armstrong; Wesley J. Barnes; Willie Clyde Beaton II; Ronnie S. Bowman, Jr.; Eean S. Cochran; Kate Louissaint; Matt Magnusson; Jodeci Milhouse; Alysha Morgan; Khadijah Rolle; Tally Sessions; Brett Sturgis; Renell Taylor; Meridien Terrell; and Dori Waymer.

Scenic and video design by Adam Koch & Steven Royal; costume design by Toni-Leslie James; lighting design by Cory Pattak; sound design by Kai Harada; wig and hair design by Matthew Armentrout; makeup design by Kali Taylor; prop design by Lilian Sun; tap choreography by Dewitt Fleming Jr.; musical direction by Darryl G. Ivey; dance music arrangement by Zane Mark; music coordination by David Lai.  At Studio 54 (254 W 54th Street). https://louisarmstrongmusical.com

While freelancing in theater production and producing, she spent 6 years as production manager at immersive theater company, Third Rail Projects, where she developed over 13 new pieces and oversaw the long-running Then She Fell. She aided in the development of new plays as Managing Director for Crashbox Theater Company from 2013-2019. She has assisted Broadway producers Jill Furman and Jed Bernstein, aiding in the reopening of the Bucks County Playhouse, and production managed opera and musical theater (during COVID!) at Manhattan School of Music. She currently works as a producer of experiential marketing and events making crazy and impossible things come to life for brands.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

What would happen if we all told the truth?   Would we recognize it?  Would we find our way to each other any more effectively than we do now, with our caution, peeking from behind our defenses, communicating in circuitous, even painfully abstract terms?   What are the ground rules for romance in the world of dating by app?  Strategic Love Play, by Miriam Battye asks these questions as it examines the existential torture of modern dating.

Jenny (Heléne Yorke) and Adam (Michael Zegen) meet in the time honored spot for a blind date – a quiet restaurant public enough for protection and intimate enough for conversation.  Well ‘conversation’ is stretching it.  It’s more an interrogation, as Jenny presents a variety of “I dare you” kinds of challenges to Adam.  Prickly and aggressive, Jenny is so clearly over the rigmarole of getting to know someone.  She is all wound, no filter, operating from a foregone conclusion go ‘it’ll never work.’   How do you avoid the self-fulflling prophecy of assuming falure?  Maybe the trick is to say “I do” to a stranger – zero expectations, zero hurt?

Arnulfo Maldonado’s excellent scenic design hints at romantic possibilities, balancing a cozy table for two within the open air of high ceilings crowned by strings of decorative lights.  Maldonado effects a clever change of scene or a passage of time with the simple expedient of a spin of the turntable on which most of the action takes place.  Space is also defined by Jen Shriever’s emotional lighting design.  The background recedes and reappears, as restaurant wall lamps alternate with deep purples of introspection, or warm oranges of hope and hesitant steps toward connection.

The play progresses through various stages of interaction, with some interesting twists and good laughs, but the material swiftly begins to feel belabored.  Katie Posner leavens the awkward, at times aggressive conversational tone with careful blocking that creates levels, but the play doesn’t really go anywhere.  Yorke and Zegen do their best but pretty quickly we find ourselves traveling back and forth over the same territory.  Yorke is given practically no arc.  She starts out quirky and insecure and travels to quirky, frightened and insecure.  We find out nothing about her.  Doesn’t she have a back story?

Zegen fares better.   His character, put on the defensive by Jenny’s relentless questions, cannot move forward so he moves inward.  Zegen finds a variety of levels and colors within that framework.  By turns overwhelmed, expressive and vulnerable, Adam develops a surprising confidence.  It’s as if a candle has been lit.  He becomes sexier, more capable of taking the initiative.

Yorke has an established presence, but her characterization becomes mannered rather quickly.  Setting up her quirkiness, reflecting the facets of her character’s protective carapace, Yorke moves through a series of engaging voices and line readings, with excellent timing.  You do wonder what Jenny is going to say next, but pretty early on you begin to see the pattern.  Jenny’s attitude becomes familiar and repetitive.  It does, however, make Yorke’s eventual outward display of vulnerability all the more striking.

The principal difficulty with Strategic Love Play is that while the premise is interesting, the story is, essentially, rather small.  Battye focuses on minute detail at the expense of a strong narrative.  There are some small discoveries but in the end it underwhelms, and doesn’t have quite enough heft to sustain the entire 75 minute run time.

Strategic Love Play by Miriam Battye, directed by Katie Posner.  With Heléne Yorke and Michael Zegen.

Set design by Arnulfo Maldonado, lighting design by Jen Schriever, costume design n by Dede Ayite, sound design by Tei Blow.

Presented by Audible, at the Minetta Lane Theatre, through December 7th.  Tickets HERE

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By David Walters
On Tuesday night November 5th, maybe you were glued to your electronic info service of choice. Maybe you couldn’t stand it all, the pressure was too much, and you went to bed at 8PM hoping to wake up to a sane world that has all but abandoned us. (Sorry didn’t happen.)
Where did I go on election night to soothe the anticipation and loosen the knot in my stomach?
Me, I was out fiddling while Rome burned.
It’s been five years since Killy “Mockstar” Dwyer was last seen in NY, but that night she appeared at the place that birthed her (Under St. Marks) for a show of fan favorites interlaced with several new outings, and up to the minute voter tally updates from her husband Craig. She said this was her swan song and she would no longer consider herself a political comic. Hah! We’ll see about that as it seems the whole world has turned into nothing but political.
She currently lives in Costa Rica (lucky her as she may be able to avoid the next four years of mayhem) and spends just as much time surfing as she does observing the world and coming up with biting and poignant songs that comment on the absurdity of it all. I’m a new fan, so I was struck by the piercing commentary in “See Something, Say Something,” “No One Respects a Slave,” “Different Colored People All Taste the Same” and “I Wanna Be a Robot.”
If you don’t know of her, you’ve basically missed a very shiny object on the underground scene. She is a musician, actor, comedian, singer, lower-east-side performance artist, MC, radio personality and proud recipient of her invented label of “Mockstar,” in all its symbolic connotations. Although you can always find her online here and here. She has been a two time Andy Kaufman award finalist, so you can get an idea of her humor from what that award heralds.
Killy has taken the yoke of freedom and is totally her, no holds barred, no pretense, unadulterated her, and that’s why she had so many fans there that night. Us in the audience that don’t grant ourselves that complete freedom to say and do whatever crosses our minds and put it out there. These were long time fans that were able to sing along with a number of her songs. There’s something to be said to have built such a following by being bizarre and weird. Something good.
For me, underground performance artists have always come across as a bit self indulgent, flailing themselves on the public dais, exposing their naughty bits (both inside and out) in order to shock, revolt, and shake us from our stupor. That’s the point though. Killy uses that sharpened point to poke holes in our lives and leaves us to examine the sore spots left behind. Bruised egos, ideas, and biases that need to be constantly examined, but we seldom do.
Killy Mockstar, hope to see you again around these parts in the not too distant future as I’m sure I’ll need some more poking.
—–
Kelly Dwyer
AKA
Killy “Mockstar” Dwyer

www.youtube.com/killythekidvids

title.rendered: Mrs. Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

Germany, 1933.  A Gestapo officer rushes a young Jewish woman into a prison cell.  A simple turn through a room in a library has brought her to the attention of the authorities.  Fresh-faced Karl and quietly intense Hannah could not, at first glance, be more different, and yet, as the interrogation proceeds along uncharacteristically conversational and philosophical lines, they discover unexpected vistas of common ground.

Hannah Stern is the philosopher Hannah Arendt, one of the foremost thinkers of the 20th century.  In Mrs. Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library, intellect and emotion travel in parallel in a subtle build that takes everyone by surprise.  Using aspects of Arendt’s real life as the basis for an examination of the fate of innocent in the face of fascism and the weaponization of thought, playwright Jenny Lyn Bader has written a beautiful, insightful story that invites us to think, challenges us to believe and opens a space for us to learn.

The actors are excellent, handling the highly literate dialogue and the play’s emotional undercurrents with equal skill.  As Karl, Brett Temple exudes innocence and vulnerability, proud of his newly gained promotion from police man to political officer, yet also confused and intimidated by the role’s responsibility.  Too new to have been warped by the system, Karl is still ‘real’ enough to be drawn out by Hannah’s gift of finding meaning in even the smallest moment.  As Hannah, in her simple dark suit and delicate pink blouse, Ella Dershowitz marries steel and glass.  Intellectual clarity grounds her fragility.  Innocent of any crime, Hannah is deeply frightened by the absurdist drama she has been thrown into.

Into her cell bursts Erich Landau (an energetic, leonine Drew Hirshfield ) an attorney who has taken it upon himself to represent Hannah – although she has never met him.  Fast talking Erich is so sure of himself, sure that his stature in the community will protect him from the ever-changing restrictions endangering the safety of all Jewish people, sure that things couldn’t possibly get worse.  Ironically, his very optimism drives home the danger of Hannah’s situation.  In a perfect reflection of the State, Erich reassures Hannah that for any argument supporting the foregone conclusion that she is guilty, he has a counterargument.  He can spin her assumed treason as cleverly disguised innocence.  Much like the Nazi State, where any action you take, they have a crime for that.  It’s an infinity loop of crazy.

Lauren Helpern set strikes just the right chord, its barren simplicity a metaphor for this time in Germany’s history.  A tiny cell with brick walls, two chairs and a clawfoot antique table – a remnant of a more human, rococo world Germany is abandoning – and windows that remain tantalizingly out of reach above.  In its near silent, twilit isolation, Hannah’s cell becomes an unlikely oasis of free thought, away from the unknown change and untold terrors outside.

Director Ari Laura Kreith builds an almost magical atmosphere with the lightest directorial hand.  Nothing is fussy.  Dialogue moves swiftly but without hurry.  Kreith maximizes the small theatre stage with compactness of movement, finding levels as Hannah reaches upward to the windows or huddles in a corner next to the room’s one small radiator.  Everything is very intentional.  And yet for all its clarity, the play brims with nuance – subtle intellectualism and even more subtle connection.  Bader paints characters in distress who remain entirely believable.  They do not veer into melodrama.

Mrs. Stern draws ingenious parallels – the creation of identities by the negation thereof.  De facto political alliances created by two diametrically opposed forces sharing the same goal.  But what does this mean in the ever-changing political landscape of Fascist Germany, where the goal posts move daily, even hourly?  As democracy dies in darkness, so justice falters with the attrition of power.  Erich has no authority, but he has agency (for now).  Karl may have authority, but he does not have agency.  Hannah has neither.

Nevertheless, amidst the chaos without and hollow doubt within,  Hannah manages to find a window of hope.  How long it will remain open is anybody’s guess.

Mrs. Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library, by Jenny Lyn Bader.  Directed by Ari Laura Kreith.  With Brett Temple, Drew Hirshfield and Ella Dershowitz.

Set design by Lauren Helpern; costume design by Deborah Caney; lighting design by Cameron Filepas; sound design by Megan Culley.

Tickets HERE.  Runtime 90 minutes with no intermission.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Victoria Lynne Dammer

The subject and acceptance of AI and its introduction to our society are as controversial as today’s politics. The Academy Award-nominated writer and director Jose Rivera has produced a timely play focusing on this dystopian view of a robotic caretaker, Stacy (Sara Koviak), perfect in every detail thanks to the newest AI algorithm, Approximation of Soul. Stacy has been hired to care for seasoned citizen Aislin (Anne O’Sullivan), a bristly old and angry woman suffering from life’s everyday wear and tear.

All technological changes are hard to transition into, and Aislin does not differ from any other human being. She has a dirtier mouth than a sailor and many unfulfilled dreams. She is toxic and has been on her own for some time. Aislin’s son has sent Stacy to assist with her burdens since he has cut her off from all communication with the world.

Stacy is programmed not to feel emotion or interfere in Aislin’s natural path. But soon, the audience senses Stacy is drawn to her client—or is she? She helps Aislin out of her shell, starts her dreaming about traveling and dating, and even suggests that she should have sex with the neighbor in her apartment building. It all appears perfect.

Yet, there are signs of Stacy’s programming malfunctioning, and you feel that something sinister will happen to Aislin as the robot almost self-destructs. Koviak is so natural as the perfect machine, Stacy, physically and unemotionally capable of performing her role with exceptional robot characteristics. O’Sullivan delivers a comical performance, grouchy yet with a sense of humor.

With all good work such as Rivera’s, we are left wondering again: Does technology improve our lives and enhance our self-worth, or are we left with the cold reality of a machine with no feelings? The crowd in the theater gets a glimpse of what might be a human side of Stacy, but is it that, or do we hope it is?

Go see Your Name Means Dream at New Jersey Repertory Company (NJ Rep), Long Branch, N.J., where they strive to present “bold, innovative works that spark conversation and thought. ” The show is now running through November 24th.

Your Name Means Dream, written and directed by Jose Rivera

WITH Sara Koviak and Anne O’Sullivan.

The Artistic Director is SuzAnne Barabas, and the Executive Director is Gabor Barabas. Your Name Means Dream is presented by a special arrangement with Paradigm Talent Agency.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“It’s time for women to take the stage.”

Is one of the themes adapter and director David Staller (who has directed every one of  of George Bernard Shaw‘s plays) puts forth in his new adaptation of Shaw’s The Devil’s Disciple.

Set in the attic of a house in New Hampshire dating from the 1700s, actress Folami Williams ushers us into the play with the plot line that she just bought the old dilapidated house (great set by Lindsay Genevieve Fuori shoehorned into the Theatre Row space) and found a journal in the attic. This construct of the historical journal was added by Staller and is not in Shaw’s play.

In this adaptation the journal was written by Judith Anderson (an original inhabitant of the house who Folami also plays) revealing the characters and plot of Shaw’s The Devil’s Disciple whose eleven characters come to life through the incantations of the journal, embodied by four ghosts that have lingered in the house through the ages. The journal construct book-ending Shaw’s play added by Staller is there to develop the theme of freedom and personal responsibility that is inherent in The Devil’s Disciple (it was banned in England for years as it reflected the troubles in Ireland at the time), as well as women’s rights both then and now. The theme of freedom is ever present today as we face the repercussions of our latest electoral process, and the struggle for women’s rights is never ending.

Does it work, this modern addition making Shaw’s play a memory play?

Yes, it does. In a large part due to the talents of the all-female cast in their character portrayals and the fun they brought to the production turning it at times into a melodrama and a farce. Through Staller’s direction they were given the freedom to play with script and the character relationships. The set, with a Narnia-inspired wardrobe cabinet that provided a portal to both the past and present, worked on several levels reflecting the many layers in the play: freedom and the world we currently live in; a moral tale of freedom set at the beginning of this country; and the rights and power of women.

Casting the play with all women added to the melodrama of this new adaptation in the characterizations, as it is written very male heavy, and it added depth to the concept of national freedom, going deeper and making it more individualistic by highlighting personal freedom in the plight of what it means to be a woman in this country (Up until 1964 an employer could refuse to hire you because you were a woman; until 1974 refusing to sell a woman a home was legal; until 1988 you could refuse to rent to a woman with children.) We’re not as advanced as we think we are.

The Devil’s Disciple is a fresh take pumping new air into one of a master playwright’s important works.

—–

The Devil’s Disciple at Theatre Row (410 W 42nd St, New York, NY 10036). Presented by Gingold Theatrical Group. Written by George Bernard Shaw and adapted and directed by David Staller. It runs through November 23, 2024 and tickets can be bought HERE.

 The cast includes Nadia Brown, Susan Cella, Tina Chilip, Teresa Avia Lim, and Folami Williams.  
 
The Devil’s Disciple features set design by Lindsay Genevieve Fuori, costume design by Tracy Christensen, lighting design by Jamie Roderick, sound design by Julian Evans, and property design by Nicole Rozanski.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

As you descend the escalator into the theater at Circle in the Square, you’ll first feel the beat of the bass; descending further, you begin to capture flashes of neon and other bright colors before glimpsing towers of speakers and colorful stuffed animals. This is your introduction to the world of Sam Gold’s  Romeo + Juliet, running for a limited, twenty week engagement on Broadway.

Gold’s adaptation of the famous story of star-crossed lovers brings the tale to a new generation.  It transports you into the dream of young love and captures the joy, delight, passion, and anguish that come with it.  Gold embraces the youthfulness of the story, supercharging it with energy and light through Jack Antonoff’s drama-inducing musical underscore and Sonya Tayeh’s vibrant movement and choreography. 

Isabella Byrd’s lighting envelops the full space, highlighting the drama and making the audience feel like they are in a nightclub infused with euphoria vibes – and it works.  Never have I ever felt so much energy and attention spanning the full two and a half hours of a Shakespearean tragedy; the audience is clapping, cheering, and singing along from moment one through the curtain call.  dots scenic design surprises and delights and Enver Chakartash’s costumes tell a story of their own for each character, highlighting familial ties and individuality.

Zegler + Connor in ROMEO + JULIET; photo by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman

The cast of characters were tantamount to keeping the audience engaged in the story.  Kit Connor captures a perfect Romeo; his eager and fresh-faced approach to the balcony scene would make anyone fall in love, and that passion extended to Romeo’s rash approach to much of the second act.  Rachel Zegler’s Juliet is grounded, and she exudes confidence and playfulness within her battle between passion and duty.  Other cast members take on multiple iconic roles giving new insight in their pairing with each other – Tommy Dorfman absolutely charms as Tybalt and the Nurse; Gabby Beans delivers a weighty performance as Mercutio, The Friar, and Prince; and Sola Fadiran garners mid-show applause in his performance as the full spectrum of Capulet parentage.

Romeo + Juliet plays with passion at its core.  Love and hate intermingle spectacularly in Gold’s production, as the young company play with power and sexuality: Capulet and Montague playfully dance and grind on each other, falling sloppily into kissing mid-punch.  Characters break into song when even the Bard’s words are not enough to underline the joy or the struggle they are feeling (Zegler’s first act closing song really brings down the house).

This Romeo + Juliet drips vibe, infusing a tone, aesthetic and perspective into the classic piece while not making the mistake of trying to do too much with the story.  The tale is as old as time, but the telling is new, exciting, and refreshed: I heard lines I had always missed, laughed harder than ever before, and was cut deeper by the young lovers’ tragedy.  A new production, one like you’ve likely never seen, with standout performances and a fabulous and aligned design team, Romeo + Juliet defies the stars and brings magic to Circle in the Square.

 

 

ROMEO + JULIET – by William Shakespeare

Direction by Sam Gold; music by Jack Antonoff; movement and choreography by Sonya Tayeh

FEATURING: Kit Connor; Rachel Zegler; Gabby Beans; Tommy Dorfman; Sola Fadiran; Taheen Modak; Gian Perez; Daniel Bravo Hernandez; Jasai Chase-Owens; and Nihar Duvvuri.

Scenic design by dots; costume design by Enver Chakartash; lighting design by Isabella Bryd; sound design by Cody Spencer; hair wig and makeup design by Robert Pickens and Katie Gell.  At Circle in the Square (235 W 50th Street).  https://romeoandjulietnyc.com/

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

I’ll just come out and say it; Dentata is back!  More specifically, vagina dentata has returned to New World Stages in TEETH, bringing with it a theatrical spectacle of music, dance, fire, rain, confetti, and plenty of severed dicks.

The musical adaptation of the 2007 cult classic film of the same name, opens Halloween for a commercial run Off-Broadway. Penned by Anna K. Jacobs and Michael R. Jackson, the show is campy and delightful, packing a deeper punch than may be expected from a cheeky, satirical comedy.

Set in the fictional town of Eden, the show centers on a group of gals who meet through a purity promise group led by the pastor and step-father of Dawn O’Keefe. O’Keefe is a perfect model of purity culture in the opening moments of the musical, encouraging her “Promise Keeper Girls” to never falter in their love of God and keep their secret “promise” safe.  However, temptation comes for all, including Dawn O’Keefe, and as things get a little hot and heavy with her high school sweetheart, she discovers that perhaps her stepbrother’s ridiculous claims may be right – maybe she does have teeth in her vagina.

The audience then follows Dawn on her journey to discover her full power as the goddess Dentata, an empowerment that is sexy and empowering and develops into a full-theater romp as Dentata and her mavens seek revenge on harmful men in a fiery, destructive rage.

The musical differs from the movie in many ways, modernizing and bringing additional diversity into the tale.  The harm of purity culture is at the forefront and we see how it harms folks in more ways than toothy privates as we follow the parallel path of Dawn’s incel stepbrother Brian, who seeks community in problematic online forums after being rejected by the church; and her best friend Ryan, a closet homosexual whose identity is continually squashed by the church (but fabulously just keeps coming out).

Alyse Alan Luis in TEETH; photo by Valerie Terranova

It’s a joy to watch this talented cast (expertly directed by Sarah Benson) simply eat up the wonderful script and score.  Alyse Alan Luis is an absolute star at Dawn O’Keefe, striking a perfect balance between button-up Promise Keeper and demented demon god – it’s a delight to go on the journey with her and watch her transition.  Andy Karl stands out as supremely over-the-top, bringing much needed humor to the church and gynecology; and the ensemble of men and women who complement the piece live fully as their characters and make wonderful, comedic choices throughout.

 

Adam Rigg’s scenic design places us in the recognizable wood-paneling and thick carpeting of a church youth group room and with the help of an amazing design team (and special effects from Jeremy Chernick) transforms it into an online chat room, a forest and lake, a gynecology office, and much more. The design of the production continues to delight and surprise throughout, matching the powerful, vibrant energy of its performers and creating a playground for Raja Feather Kelly‘s cheeky and energetic choreography.

TEETH is charming, funny, poignant, timely, and a piece that you can really sink your teeth into (wherever you may have them).  Don’t try to resist temptation, make your way to New World Stages to see the show!

 

TEETH – Anna K. Jacobs, book and music; Michael R. Jackson, book and lyrics

Directed by Sarah Benson; Choreography by Raja Feather Kelly

FEATURING: Alyse Alan Luis; Andy Karl; Will Connolly; Jason Gotay; Jared Loftin; Courtney Bassett; Jenna Rose Husli; Michaela Lamas; Madison McBride; Sydney Parra; & Wren Rivera,

Scenic design by Adam Rigg; costumes by Enver Chakartash; lighting by Jane Cox & Stacey Derosier; sound by Palmer Hefferan; special effects by Jeremy Chernick.  AtNew Work Stages: 340 West 50th Street. https://teeththemusical.com/

title.rendered: Little House on the Ferry: The Musical

content.rendered:
Little House on the Ferry: The Musical and Heartfelt Celebration of Universal Love

By Edward Kliszus

In a world where identity, politics, and love intersect, Little House on the Ferry: The Musical offers a whimsical yet profound exploration of LGBTQ+ life, friendship, and the fight for equality at Ferry’s Landing. Written by Rob Gould, with music and lyrics by Gould and Rob Arbelo, the production weaves a tale of self-discovery and community against the stunning backdrop of Fire Island and the impending 2011 Marriage Equality Act vote in the Albany Senate. Directed by Victoria Rae Sook and choreographed by Michael McCrary, Little House on the Ferry is as sentimental as fun, filled with laughter, heartwarming moments, and a sense of connection.

Felipe Galganni : Xana DuMe – Photo by Austin Ruffer

Entertaining and Interactive

From the moment the lights dim and the first notes play, the extraordinarily entertaining and interactive Little House on the Ferry sweeps viewers into a seamless world of artistry, precision, and heart. The production’s stagecraft is a marvel, featuring impeccably timed entrances, exits, and clever banter that keep the narrative crisp and lively. Every line feels meticulously placed, enhancing both comedic and tender moments, while the energetic pacing never falters, creating an irresistible rhythm that draws the audience deeper into the story.

(L-R) Kelsey Rogers, Kailin Brown, and Manuela Agudelo – Photo by Austin Ruffer

Greek Chorus Trio

The Greek chorus trio—Kailin Brown, Manuela Agudelo, and Kelsey Rogers add a unique layer of vibrancy and flair. The trio delivers precise, synchronized movements, punctuating key moments with style and energy. Powerful dance routines are meticulously choreographed, each step a testament to their skill and cohesion. The trio’s dances bring a dynamic rhythm to the production, accentuating pivotal scenes and amplifying humor and drama. Xana DuMe, portrayed by Felipe Galganni, elevates the performance with extraordinary and captivating tap sequences. Galganni’s tap dancing is as polished as it is spirited, each click and stomp adding flair to Xana’s larger-than-life personality. Combining the trio’s powerful dancing and Xana’s dazzling tap routines turned the stage into a vibrant spectacle, merging technical excellence with pure entertainment.

Charles Osborne (Center) and Little House on the Ferry Cast – Photo by Austin Ruffer

The choreography by Michael McCrary is a true standout. It blends joyful group numbers with intimate duets that capture the essence of each character’s journey. Movements flow naturally from scene to scene as dance becomes a powerful extension of the emotional highs and lows. Meanwhile, Tyler Mark Holland‘s costumes bring Fire Island’s spirited diversity to life, with Xana DuMe’s glamorous outfits and snappy sensu stealing the spotlight and every ensemble capturing the characters’ personalities on stage.

A Scene from Little House on the Ferry. Courtesy ferryslandingnyc.com

Dynamic Group Pieces

The vocal harmonies are equally impressive. The cast’s layered voices blend seamlessly, adding depth and richness to each musical number, from soul-stirring solos to dynamic group pieces. Combined with Rob Gould and Rob Arbelo’s clever, heartfelt lyrics, the music feels both timeless and fun, with upbeat tunes and reflective ballads that are deeply resonant.

Under Zach Pizza’s expert lighting design, each scene is bathed in hues that reflect the emotional temperature, shifting seamlessly from warm, beachy tones to cooler, introspective lighting for more intimate moments. Sound is equally well-engineered, amplifying the emotional impact and ensuring no nuance is lost. The result is a fully immersive experience that captures the soul of Fire Island and resonates long after the final bow.

Christopher Harrod and Charles Osborne – Photo by Austin Ruffer

A Fire Island Story About Love, Politics, and Self-Acceptance

The story takes place on Fire Island during a pivotal weekend when four friends—Randall, Timothy, Jake, and Donnie—gather for what seems like a carefree getaway. As they bask in the sun and sip Planter’s Punch, the looming New York Marriage Equality vote casts a shadow over their weekend of relaxation. Randall (played by Charles Osborne) is the hopeful optimist, while Timothy (Andrew Leggieri) remains cautious and unsure about his relationship and future.

Personal and Political Journeys Intertwine in a Rich Emotional Story

In addition to the political undertones, each character’s journey of self-discovery and acceptance forms the story’s emotional core. Jake (Troy Valjean Rucker) exudes confidence, while Donnie (Christopher Harrod) adds comic relief with his endearing self-deprecation. Yet, despite their differences, the four friends share a profound bond that makes the play’s exploration of a chosen family all the more poignant.

Felipe Galganni : Xana DuMe and Troy Valjean Rucker – Photo by Austin Ruffer Large

A Vibrant Drag Queen and Greek Chorus Add Magic to the Storytelling

At the center of the chaos is the show’s vibrant drag queen narrator, Xana DuMe, portrayed with dazzling flair by Felipe Galganni. Xana is the glue that holds the group together, offering wisdom, humor, and some show-stopping numbers. The Greek chorus, played by Kailin Brown, Manuela Agudelo, and Kelsey Rogers, adds a surreal yet insightful layer, guiding both the characters and the audience through the emotional landscape of the story through dance, song, and ubiquitous show-stopping costume changes.

Music and Lyrics: Add Heart and Humor to the Story

Rob Gould and Rob Arbelo’s musical score is one of the production’s highlights. Each song enhances the narrative while capturing the characters’ essence and experiences. Standout numbers like “Jump That Fence” and “Planter’s Punch Dreams” are catchy, fun, and packed with witty lyrics. These songs capture the carefree spirit of Fire Island and the complexities of friendship, love, and acceptance.

Direction and Choreography Seamlessly Blend Emotion and Energy

Victoria Rae Sook’s direction is both sensitive and lively, perfectly balancing the humorous and serious moments. She uses the intimate space at Ferry’s Landing to create a personal and immersive show. Under her guidance, the characters shine in their arcs while maintaining a cohesive group dynamic.

High energy on stage in Little House on the Ferry. Courtesy ferryslandingnyc.com

Choreography Elevates the Emotional Highs and Lows of the Story

Choreographer Michael McCrary adds another layer of energy to the production with vibrant dance sequences that mirror the emotional highs and lows of the story. The beachside dance numbers, for example, are joyful and carefree, while the more intimate movements during quieter moments reflect the characters’ vulnerability. McCrary’s choreography feels organic, seamlessly integrated into the fabric of the narrative rather than serving as a mere spectacle.

Stellar Cast Brings the Characters’ Emotional Journeys to Life

The cast of Little House on the Ferry is nothing short of stellar. Charles Osborne, as Randall, delivers a performance full of charm and optimism, making him the show’s emotional anchor. Andrew Leggieri, as Timothy, provides a nuanced portrayal of a man grappling with his fears of love and commitment. Their chemistry is palpable, adding authenticity to the story’s emotional core.

(L-R) Kailin Brown, Manuela Agudelo, and Kelsey Rogers – Photo by Austin Ruffer Large

Donnie and Jake Add Humor and Depth to the Ensemble

Troy Valjean Rucker as Jake and Christopher Harrod as Donnie bring humor and depth to the production. Rucker’s confidence contrasts perfectly with Harrod’s self-deprecating humor, creating a balance that allows for moments of levity even in the play’s more serious scenes.

Felipe Galganni’s Xana DuMe Steals the Show with Heart and Humor

However, it’s Felipe Galganni, as Xana DuMe steals the show. Galganni’s performance is bold, campy, and full of heart. Xana’s larger-than-life persona adds fun and wisdom to the story, guiding the audience and the characters. Xana’s Greek chorus, portrayed by Kailin Brown and Manuela Agudelo, adds a whimsical element that keeps the narrative moving smoothly.

Little House on the Ferry Cast – Photo by Austin Ruffer

Visuals and Design Bring Fire Island to Life on Stage

The design elements in Little House on the Ferry are nothing short of a visual feast. Shawn Lewis’s set design transports the audience to the sunny shores of Fire Island, using vibrant colors and clever staging to evoke the laid-back, beachside atmosphere. The set design is minimal but effective, allowing the actors to take center stage while creating a vivid sense of place.

Extravagant Costumes and Dynamic Lighting Elevate the Atmosphere

Another highlight is Tyler Mark Holland’s costume design, especially regarding Xana DuMe’s extravagant outfits. Each costume is thoughtfully crafted to reflect the characters’ personalities, from the casual beachwear to the drag queen’s show-stopping ensembles. Zach Pizza’s lighting design enhances the mood of each scene, using soft, romantic lighting for intimate moments and brighter, energetic hues for the upbeat musical numbers.

(Front Row) Andrew Leggieri, Charles Osborne and Gilberto Saenz – Photo by Austin Ruffer

The Production Team

Anthony Francavilla – General Manager
Quenton Ellis Music – Director/Music Producer
Corey Kline Music – Producer
Michael McCrary – Choreographer
Courtney Darling – Associate Choreographer
Zach Pizza – Lighting Design
Ryk Lewis – Sound Design
Shawn Lewis – Scenic Design
Indigo – Costume Design
Grace Griffin – Stage Manager
Michele Miles – Assistant Stage Manager
Eric Nightengale – Production Manager
Sydney Scott – Production Assistant

Ferry’s Landing: The Perfect Venue for Immersive Entertainment

The significance of Little House on the Ferry is not just in its story but also in the venue where it is being performed. The Duplex, a historic venue home for performers and artists since the 1960s, is reopening after suffering fire damage in 2022. Now, under the banner of Ferry’s Landing, the venue is set to reestablish itself as a center for immersive entertainment. Ferry’s landing access can be accessed through The Duplex, 59 Christopher St, New York, NY 10014.

For tickets and information, click HERE.

If you enjoyed diving into the world of Little House on the Ferry, you’ll be captivated by our other in-depth theater reviews. Discover more insights, standout performances, and must-see productions. Don’t miss out—explore our latest reviews and recommendations HERE for your next unforgettable theater experience!

title.rendered: Strike Up the Band at Carnegie Hall

content.rendered:
Strike Up the Band at Carnegie Hall

By Edward Kliszus

On a crisp October evening, Strike Up the Band brilliantly illuminated Carnegie Hall’s Isaac Stern Auditorium. This dazzling revival, presented by the superb MasterVoices chorus and orchestra and helmed by the visionary impresario Ted Sperling, brought a new vitality to this 1927 Gershwin operetta. Originally an anti-war satire, the piece returned to the stage with a spirit that felt both timeless and remarkably relevant. Indeed, tonight, we celebrate Strike Up the Band: A Spectacular Revival of Gershwin’s Masterpiece.

Melodic Prowess of Gershwin’s Work

Notably, the production featured an impressive lineup of guest artists, each of whom coupled humor with profound musicality, dance, and drama. Moreover, the cast reaffirmed the Gershwin brothers’ genius throughout the performance. The production not only embraced the satirical sharpness of George S. Kaufman’s original book but highlighted the melodic prowess of George and Ira Gershwin’s unforgettable compositions. This review captures the essence of a truly magnificent performance that invited the audience to reflect on the state of modern society, all while reveling in top-notch theatrical artistry.

Strike Up The Band (1927 original production) Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A Timely Revival with Timeless Themes

Ted Sperling, conductor and director of Strike Up the Band, chose this work deliberately. With only days to go until a tense national election, the operetta’s themes of politics, patriotism, and the absurdity of war felt more resonant than ever. As Sperling noted in his pre-show conversation with co-writer Laurence Maslon, the satire embedded within the play couldn’t be more on point for today’s audiences. Kaufman’s biting humor, initially crafted in the wake of World War I, struck a deep chord with contemporary viewers. The play’s premise—an absurd war over cheese tariffs—allowed Kaufman and the Gershwins to explore the follies of blind patriotism and rampant consumerism, themes that echo meaningfully in today’s world.

The Final Jewel in MasterVoices’ Gershwin Series

In a conversation between Sperling and Maslon, the director shared his excitement about finally presenting this piece as the “final jewel” in MasterVoices’ exploration of the Gershwins’ political satires. Sperling says, “We all need a good laugh, some tap dancing, and gorgeous melodies.” His statement resonated throughout the performance; every humorous twist in Strike Up the Band held a layer of sincerity, ultimately making this production entertaining and thought-provoking.

Rialto Theatre advertisement for the American musical film Strike Up the Band (1940) – 10 Oct. 1940 Morning Call, Allentown PA. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A Star-Studded Cast and Impeccable Performances

The cast brought the characters of Strike Up the Band to life with palpable energy and finesse. In the role of Horace J. Fletcher, the ambitious CEO of Fletcher’s American Cheese Company, John Ellison Conlee infused the character with charm and absurdity, perfectly embodying the capitalist satire at the heart of the story. His interactions with Shereen Ahmed as Joan Fletcher, his daughter, and Bryce Pinkham as Jim Townsend, a local journalist and Joan’s love interest, were humorous and dynamic. Conlee’s comedic timing and bold delivery of Fletcher’s bombastic lines and puns about milk and cheese consistently elicited laughter from the audience, grounding the satire in a relatable human experience.

Warmth and Gravitas in Every Note

As the well-intentioned philanthropist Mrs. Draper, Victoria Clark brought warmth and gravitas to her role. Her performance, particularly during the song “If I Became the President,” showcased her nuanced ability to blend humor with sincerity, making her character one of the most memorable in the production. Meanwhile, Bryce Pinkham’s portrayal of Jim Townsend served as an anchor in the whirlwind of satire, embodying a journalist whose love for Joan Fletcher pushes him to question the motives behind Fletcher’s business-driven war.

Additionally, Christopher Fitzgerald shined as George Spelvin, an eccentric ambassador, delivering his lines with the wit and playfulness for which he is celebrated. His performance with the dancers in “Mademoiselle in New Rochelle” added a lightheartedness that beautifully contrasted with the satirical weight of the plot.

L-R: Portraits of George and Ira Gershwin. Photo of G. Gershwin by Carl Van Vechten. Photos Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A Standout Production Design and Choreography

Every detail of this production, from the costumes to the lighting, contributed to the grandeur and charm of the evening. Choreographer Alison Solomon captured the energy and humor of the show’s musical numbers, presenting tap dance and ensemble choreography that honored the period while feeling fresh and lively. Each dance number became a visual spectacle, perfectly complementing the operetta’s blend of satire and nostalgia.

Satirical Portrayal Enhanced by Costumes and Lighting

The production design, led by co-costume designers Tracy Christensen and Somie Pak, transported the audience back to a 1927 America bursting with patriotism and commercial ambition. Costumes for characters like Fletcher and Mrs. Draper were meticulously tailored, adding authenticity to the satirical portrayal of their characters. Additionally, Shelby Loera’s lighting design effectively shifted between the show’s lighter, comedic scenes and its darker moments of introspection. In moments like the song “Oh, This Is Such a Lovely War,” Loera’s lighting underscored the gravity behind the humor, casting shadows that hinted at the darker implications of war.

Sound Design That Merges Grand and Intimate

Marc Salzberg’s sound design was pivotal in bringing the rich orchestration to life. The MasterVoices Orchestra, under Sperling’s baton, filled Carnegie Hall with the Gershwin brothers’ iconic melodies. Orchestrations by Russell Warner, William D. Brohn, William Daly, Dick Hyman, Sid Ramin, Larry Wilcox, and Donald Johnston breathed life into each number, creating a full-bodied soundscape that felt grand yet intimate.

Strike Up the Band (1940 film) MGM, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Celebrating Gershwin’s Musical Genius

At the heart of Strike Up the Band lies George Gershwin’s timeless score, enriched by Ira Gershwin’s clever lyrics that capture the essence of love in its many forms. Exquisitely beautiful songs like “The Man I Love” and “I’ve Got a Crush on You” were delivered with profound emotion and delightful wit, showcasing the Gershwin brothers’ exceptional talent in merging melody with satire. Shereen Ahmed and Bryce Pinkham, as Joan Fletcher and Jim Townsend, brought these love songs to life, their voices blending seamlessly as they delivered each gentle intone with elegance and conviction.

Heartfelt Renditions of Universal Love

The universal nature of love—its hope, longing, and gentle humor—was felt deeply through their duets. Ahmed’s tender yet vibrant soprano complemented Pinkham’s resonant tenor, creating a chemistry that drew the audience into their unfolding romance. Their heartfelt renditions captured love’s quiet, soulful moments and grand, sweeping gestures, reminding the audience that love can bloom amidst the absurdity of a satirical cheese war.

Unyielding Power of Love in Every Note

Viewers were entranced as the pair expressed a love that transcends place and time, rich with spirit, charm, and humor. Many in the audience held their breath, sighing in unison as the two sang each deliciously romantic line, enveloping the room with a sense of shared humanity. The songs became more than melodies; they became expressions of an enduring truth—the unyielding power of love, even in the face of conflict and absurdity. This masterful interpretation left an indelible mark, reinforcing that love remains universal and transcendent, no matter the setting.

This thoughtfully directed production, under Ted Sperling’s leadership, honored the Gershwins’ legacy by focusing on the play’s deeper themes without sacrificing its humor, romance, or charm.

Strike Up the Band at Carnegie Hall presented by Master Voices. Photo by Edward Kliszus

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Another Shot focuses on the decision to go through rehab versus deciding to BE in rehab. It’s easy to go through the motions, and Harry (Dan Butler), Chicago radio personality and a former alcoholic, thinks his best bet is to get through a few weeks of rehab and get back to work for the sole purpose of saving his chances of returning to his job. Another Shot is loosely based on the real-life experiences of Harry Teinowitz, whose career and life were put in jeopardy following an arrest for DUI.

Other residents at the rehabilitation center, Vince (Chiké Johnson), Isaiah (Gregg Mozgala), Andrea (Samantha Mathis), and George (Quentin Nguyễn-duy), become not only friends but a support system. Another Shot emphasizes the foundation of recovery, the days and weeks that feel like an eternity without your vice.

Photo Credit: Joan Marcus

Vince, a motivator for the other three guys, seems to be the strongest, most committed, and confident in his future self: a sober husband and father. Isaiah, a former pharmacist and pill addict, tells the men that his fiancé is waiting for him on the outside, that she’s the one that forced him to come: it was either her or the pills. We’re surprised when lies are revealed; they’re unexpected, told out of shame.

Andrea has been both married and in rehab a handful of times. We see her commitment to be in rehab through her maturity and acknowledgment or her actions. She almost seems like a senior rehab-ber. We hope this time will be her last.

George, is the youngest with numerous instances of drinking while in rehab—we see the endless support the other residents give him, the support and chances Therapist Barb(Portia) (also a former alcoholic) gives him. We see the hope Barb has in all of them; we see the hope they have for each other—more than they seemingly have for themselves at times. Maybe it’s easier to cheer on others, to believe in their capabilities rather than ourselves.

Photo Credit: Joan Marcus

Between scenes of random days of Harry being in rehab, there are clips of voices speaking, telling their personal anecdotes about the moments they realized they needed sobriety. While these clips were meant to serve as a comedic break, a transition between days in rehab, they felt as though they detracted from the real importance of humor used in the play.

In fact, I question whether these clips of voices are true, if their speakers have lived these experiences. If not, or even since this is not clear, it takes away even more from the importance of the topic of alcoholism.

Harry’s humor functions in the play as a coping mechanism, a way to avoid the seriousness of alcoholism, the seriousness of sobriety. It highlights how people avoid talking about sobriety, how people—like Harry—treat embarrassing and negatively-impacting drunken experiences as a funny story. His humor attempts to hide the emotion and shame, the regret with habitually making the choice to do the same thing over and over again each night, each event, each afternoon with the guys at the bar.

Harry says that “therapy feels like a “colonoscopy in the middle of a food court.” There’s nowhere to hide. Comedic lines sprinkled throughout the performance highlight Harry’s personality but also becomes a way to show Harry’s growth as he grows from avoiding the acknowledgment of the impact of alcoholism to using humor to connect through alcoholism.

And Harry soon realizes the long-term effects of alcohol; it becomes a shot he “can’t pay.” Thinking about when drinking was fun is like forgetting the rest.

We watch each addict rise an crumble and make it from one day to the next; but we question whether they will all overcome their emotional and mental challenges. “Everything you love can fit into a single shot glass.”

Because you can lose it all that quickly.

ANOTHER SHOT, Co-written Spike Manton and Harry Teinowitz; Directed by Jackson Gay.

WITH Dan Butler (Harry); Chiké Johnson (Vince); Samantha Mathis (Andrea); Gregg Mozgala (Isaiah); Quentin Nguyễn-duy (George); and Portia (Barb).

CREATIVE TEAM: Beowulf Boritt (Scenic Design), Mextly Couzin (Lighting Design),  Daniel Baker (Sound Design), Stefania Bulbarella (Projection Design), Alejo Vietti (Costume Design), Donald Cameron Clark, Jr. (Producer), Laura Stanczyk (Exectuive Producer).

Another Shot is playing at the Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre at the Signature Center, 480 W 42nd St, New York, NY, until Saturday, January 4, 2025.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

This fall, with Halloween almost here, many scarier things are happening in this country and the world than what any ghouls and goblins can conjure up to fright me. One is Atlas Drugged, by The Builders Association, which ran for only three shows at NYU Skirball. If you’re aware of the politics around you, this will scare your pants off.

In the shadowy landscape of 2028 (a little ways away but right around the corner and too close for comfort) manipulation is happening without us even realizing it.  Silicon Valley unleashes a chilling creation: an AI-driven political candidate forged from the sinister doctrines of Ayn Rand and the alt-right’s darkest ideologies. This candidate is meticulously crafted to resonate with its audience, any audience, engineered and tested with harrowing new campaign strategies and twisted strains of political messaging all geared to speak directly to you personally. The world of this close future unfolds like a twisted carnival, highlighted by a sinister game show, Power Play! (a game show about money and power that the audience plays along with on their phones) that highlights the little know facts about how we brought ourselves to this place, today, and the terrifying future that very well may await us all.

The theatrical company The Builders Association (which examines the impact of media on cultures and communities) feels like they’re breathing down our necks, warning us about what’s to come in this world premiere production. Leaping off of Ann Rand’s Atlas Shrugged, Atlas Drugged creates an AI-blended world where they develop our new political leader, an amalgam of what we each want to hear. To say that watching the production made me a little scared and nauseous (more than I am already) about what could possibly be, would be an understatement. We are being manipulated more and more without realizing it. Influenced without our knowledge.

In this highly technological show (like being inside a computer), it’s both fascinating and scary to watch as the technicians take pieces from Ayn Rand, Mr. Rogers, Dolly Parton, Glenda the Good Witch of the North, and Taylor Swift, add in fascist totalitarian ideas, and blend them into the ultimate political candidate that, with our blessing, becomes our Big Brother world. It’s all too close to home.

This show is the ultimate “To hold as ’twere the mirror up to nature.” Do you like what you see?

—–

Atlas Drugged is directed by Marianne Weems, and writer/dramaturgy by James Gibbs.

Set and costume design by Andreea Mincic; video design by Autin Switser; sound design by Dan Dobson; lighting design by Jennifer Tipton and Allen Hahn; and media architecture and design by Lawrence Shea.

It is performed by Moe Angelos and Tanya Selvaratnam.

Do keep tabs on The Builders Association for what’s coming next as they do have their theatrical stethoscope keenly attuned to our current society.

title.rendered: Sunset Blvd. reviewed Betsyann Faiella Oct. 23

content.rendered:
Oxford Languages defines theater as a play or other activity or presentation considered in terms of its dramatic quality.

By this definition, I give Jamie Lloyd’s Sunset Blvd., a 5 out of 5. It’s a visual spectacle from which my attention never waned. This Norma Desmond, this version of the show, has entered contemporary territory. The production is stripped down to bare bones with a minimal set (it is mainly a large black box), embellished and enhanced by lighting, fog, and live cinematography projected on small and large screens on stage and above. There are 21st C. references to film, social media…and this Norma also twerks. The score is the familiar score (minus “The Lady’s Paying” and “Eternal Youth Is Worth a Little Suffering”), with gorgeous, haunting, extremely fluid singing from the startling talent, Nicole Scherzinger. There is no grand, deteriorating staircase, there are no turbans. There is one fierce/fragile, deluded, exposed creature, barefoot in a black slip-dress throughout, her love interest, Joe (Tom Francis), and her faithful and protective man-servant/former husband, Max (David Thaxton), who exhibits a most touching display of raw emotion late in the show. The supporting cast and dancers/singers play their parts well. In this production, though, I could almost have done without the Betty (Grace Hodgett Young) and Joe story. It is perfunctory, and not as if Joe is besotted with Betty. Betty is just another (possible) port in the storm, like Norma’s driveway or the free room above the garage at Sunset Blvd. If you’re going to strip it down, why not go all the way?

Throughout, besides her elegant singing, Scherzinger displays fluid movement, and expertise with opposition acting. In the same sentence, a kitten-like quality becomes a lion’s roar, a delicate and bereft creature becomes a confident, dry and direct businesswoman, a silent era film star expertly slips into 21st Century vocal fry.

Tom Francis’s down and out Joe Gillis is kind. He is somewhat under Norma’s spell, waiting for the money that was promised and knowing he should bail out, but drawn back in when Norma attempts suicide. He’s handsome and boyish, frequently shown in closeup, and showcased in a live sequence immediately after intermission when a camera follows him through the bowels of the St. James Theater and out onto the street. He poses next to a life-size picture of himself; Norma’s dead pet chimp joins the entourage briefly. This sequence adds to the production’s new filmic territory as fantasy and reality mix. Are they really in the street? Was it pre-recorded? I wasn’t sure, frankly (it was live).

I think it’s worth mentioning the chatter about whether Scherzinger is too young to play the role. Scherzinger is mirrored frequently by an actress playing her younger self (who resembles her not at all in body type or visage). It enhances the misogynistic territory of the script. Hollywood generally disdains women who are older than 30. Very few women of Scherzinger’s age (46) were considered bankable until recent years, when many female stars began speaking out about ageism, and others founded production successful production companies of their own to tell their stories. So, I find her casting in this contemporary production to be an example of synergy rather than dissonance.

The orchestra was superb. When the audience spilled out onto 44th Street after the final curtain, many seemed dazed and had to be coaxed out of the middle of the road by police and security.

Nicole Scherzinger as Norma Desmond rules, from an image on a 23-foot screen to her frail figure in the foggy and dimly lit set. The director and producers took a tired show and re-made it for a contemporary audience. It doesn’t pack an emotional wallop. It packs a creative one.

Credits: Sunset Blvd. is a re-imagining by director Jamie Lloyd of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Boulevard. With book and lyrics by Don Black and Christopher Hampton, and based on the Paramount Pictures film directed by Billy Wilder.

WITH: Nicole Scherzinger as Norma Desmond, Tom Francis as Joe Gillis, Grace Hodgett Young as Betty Schaefer, David Thaxton as Max Von Mayerling. Mandy Gonzalez guest stars as Norma Desmond at certain select performances and Caroline Bowman is standby for the role of Norma Desmond.

Ensemble members: Olivia Lacie Andrews, Brandon Mel Borkowsky, Shavey Brown, Hannah Yun Chamberlain, Cydney Clark, Raúl Contreras, Tyler Davis, E.J. Hamilton, Sydney Jones, Emma Lloyd, Pierre Marais, Shayna McPherson, Jimin Moon, Justice Moore, Drew Redington, Diego Andres Rodriguez, Swing: Giuseppe Bausilio (dance captain), Kristina Garvida Doucette (assistant dance captain), Brandon LaVar, Maggie Likcani, Abby Matsusaka, and Rixey Terry.

Soutra Gilmour (set and costume design), Fabian Aloise (choreography), Alan Williams (music supervisor and music director), Jack Knowles (lighting design), Adam Fisher (sound design), Nathan Amzi and Joe Ransom (video design and cinematography), Cheryl Thomas (hair and makeup design), Ann James (intimacy coordinator).

At the St. James Theatre.  TICKETS

title.rendered: In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot ~ A Non-Review

content.rendered:
FROM THE EDITOR:

Dear Reader – In the interest of full disclosure I am writing to let you know that The Front Row Center will not be reviewing “In The Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot” because I, Tulis McCall, am a member of this cast as well as being the Editor of The Front Row Center.  This creates a conflict of interest.

Unlike our Supreme Court, we are sensitive to conflicts of interest at FRC.  An FRC reviewer who knows anyone involved in a production normally recuses themselves from reviewing said production.  In this case that recusal would apply to the entire bunch of writers for FRC.  No writers equals no review.

You will find information on the play below.  We thank you in advance for your understanding and hope to see you at the theatre!

* * * * * *

As the oceans rise, a band of queer warehouse workers travel from job to job, running from the encroaching coastline. An unlikely love story, and a startling new work of speculative fiction, In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot is a quietly revolutionary tale of queer aging, chosen family, and the search for home in a volatile world.

FROM THE DIRECTOR SIVAN BATTAT:

“A lot of the people who are forced to live as itinerant workers are doing so because they don’t have other choices, because our country has fundamentally failed them… One thing in your life can go wrong and suddenly you’re stuck in a cycle, doing manual labor into your 70s. These characters have had no path out of class struggle. One of the most important things about the play is how this community has formed as a result of that—that no one, structurally speaking, is looking out for us, so we’ll do it for each other.”

FROM THE WRITER SARAH MANTELL: “Women, trans, and nonbinary artists deserve to be center stage. The canon has always held white male actors from cradle to grave and we deserve those kinds of futures, too. I have been reliably informed that this was one of the most extensive casting processes in Playwrights Horizons’ history, and I believe it. Come see what our extraordinary company of artists has made. Similarly, I haven’t seen a lot of playwrights who the field perceives as female get a career break over the age of 40. It’s something I have honestly been scared about—and I don’t know if I would have had the chance to put a play like this into the theatre world in this big way if I was perceived as closer to the age of my characters.”

“In The Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot” won the prestigious Susan Smith Blackburn Prize last year. Now it hits the stage for the first time at Playwrights Horizons (which commissioned it) featuring a multi-generational cast.

In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot runs approximately 90 minutes with no intermission.

Playwrights Horizons and Breaking the Binary Theatre present Sarah Mantell‘s In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot. Sivan Battat is directing.

—-

The cast: Barsha (formerly known as Debra Barsha) as Horowitz, Sandra Caldwell as El, Donnetta Lavinia Grays as Jen, Ianne Fields Stewart as Sara, Deirdre Lovejoy as Ani, Tulis McCall as Ash, and Pooya Mohseni as Maribel.

The scenic design is by Emmie Finckel, costume design by Mel Ng, lighting design by Cha See, and sound design by Sinan Refik Zafar. The creative team also includes voice, text, and dialect coach Gigi Buffington.

Tickets are on sale at PlaywrightsHorizons.org.  Through November 17.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“This group is as real as it gets.”

Rawshock crafts a safe place, a space of trust and care and support. Five individuals—some inpatient and some outpatients at a mental health hospital—meet for group. They share their histories, their traumas, their hopes.

Group is about relating to each other, comforting each other, being present. Liz (Camber Carpenter), a therapist of sorts, is the leader of group. She’s dedicated to Group, committed to keep it running at all costs. When an incident occurs, she chooses not to report it, protecting both the members of the group and the group’s operation. But we wonder how long Group can last when a power struggle arises when a new doctor enters the hospital.

Dr. Sam Rosen (David Silberger) is a character immediately disliked—his crumpled suits and his intentions with the hospital are equally bad.

Alex (Nathan Cusson) is angry but sweet; he’s an outpatient. He blames himself for his mother’s death, and he expresses his deep, emotional pain.

Tina (Chelsea Clark) is quiet, frightened, and suffering from crippling anxiety. We first meet her as she’s polishing windows with a cloth she always carries, a method of coping. She believes she is responsible for her brother being put into the foster care system. Tina, also an outpatient, is spends Group preparing for and dreading an interview. Will her anxiety overtake her?

Dana (Jennifer Pierro) is loud. She has stopped taking her medication, and she uses music as a coping mechanism. She thinks she killed her parents’ dreams as their child.

Katherine (Theresa Della Valle), a long-term resident, is grandmother to everyone in the group, handing out Domino sugar packets and congratulating everyone’s victories, crying for their trials. She is ashamed of herself, rich, and no longer has a relationship with her own daughter. Group members have become like her adopted children, others she can cheer lead and share in honesty with.

Richard (Christian Libonati), a male prostitute living on the streets has a business degree and an abusive father. He is the newest member of Group; he keeps to himself and is reluctant to share his trauma and feelings. Richard is hesitant to even make eye contact; but he’s here for each session and we watch his personal growth and develop a hope of healing for him, along with the others.

The five members’ outbursts and actions are extreme,  sudden, and unhinged at times. Their performance is superb, real. I am so pleasantly surprised; this show is a must-see. Rawshock’s depth and heaviness highlights the need for mental health outlets for support; it shows the failures of mental health facilities.

I’m rooting for each member of Group to make it, to heal, to accomplish what they may not have been capable of without this group. I’m rooting for Group. The necessity and importance of groups like this one is emphasized throughout the performance, as characters take steps both backwards and forwards, as they all hold each other up. I urge you to pack the house and see this performance in the time it remains at The Chain Theater.

Written by Rita Lewis; Directed and Produced by Ken Wolf.

CAST: Jennifer Pierro (Dana), Camber Carpenter (Liz), David Silberger (Dr. Sam Rosen), Nathan Cusson (Alex), Theresa Della Valle (Katherine), Chelsea Clark (Tina), Christian Libonati (Richard).

Rawshock is presented by Manhattan Repertory Theatre. It is playing until Nov. 3, 2024 at The Chain Theater, 312 West 36 Street, Floor 4, New York, NY.

Tickets can be purchased here.
