content.rendered:
by Brittany Crowell

Left on Tenth by Delia Ephron, sister of (and often co-author with) the late queen of rom-coms, Nora Ephron, is a play about totality: it’s about finding love after loss and being brave enough to give in to it; about living life to its fullest; about hope and second chances.  Based on her bestselling memoir of the same name, the piece is told as a first person narrative from Delia’s perspective, but in translation from page to stage, it loses a lot of its heart.

Julianna Margulies’ Delia presents us the story with an affected, child-like enthusiasm that feels both jarring and unnatural.  Her partner in crime Peter, played by Peter Gallagher, is slightly less affected but performs with the same over-the-top energy that hits just short of humor or charm.  

I wanted so badly to fall in love with this couple falling in love; to be on the journey with them, but as Delia recounts moment and moment, memory and memory, it never breaches the surface or connects deeply with the audience.  Instead of feeling charming and inspiring, the courting of these two characters feels performative and too-good-to-be-true; with the lovers represented as unrealistically perfect and perfect for each other. What I’m sure is a moving, personal and vulnerable novel loses much in its translation to the stage; posing the question: Why does this need to be theater?  How is the story enhanced by the theatricality of its telling?  My answer upon reviewing: it doesn’t, and it’s not.

Our two stars are complemented by two actors who take on multiple costume changes and demeanors to fill out the cast of characters supporting Delia (Peter Francis James and Kate MacCluggage). James brings a fun yet goofy energy while MacLuggage’s characters appear more reserved and refined.  Our two featured actors fit in with the affected stars but the overall silliness of their tone clunks awkwardly against the seriousness of parts of the narrative and doesn’t allow for the audience to connect with the characters along their journey.

That’s not to say that there were no moments of joy and feeling in the piece: Margulies brings us a heart-wrenching scene from her hospital bed when her body wants to give up, and my throat tightened as she confronted the diagnosis of the same disease as her sister; Peter Francis James performs a moving and humorous revelation from a neighbor with HIV; and Gallagher puts it all on the table as he fights for his love to survive.

All that being said, the most satisfying element of the piece is almost the set, designed by Beowulf Boritt, the piece opens on a Who’s Got Mail-esque library and morphs (often through the help of stunning projection design by Jeanette Oi-Suk Yew) into Central Park, the World Trade Center, a West Village Cafe, an interstate in the west, and much more.  When the script begins to shift to a more serious tone in the second half, the whole set makes a literal 360 and gives us a hospital room, but even then Boritt and Yew find creative ways to bring color and energy to the scene. 

Everyone loves a good love story and everyone loves a story about conquering the odds, second chances, and living life to its fullest.  Unfortunately Delia Ephron’s Left of Tenth simply doesn’t satisfy, be it the over-stylized performances, or the too-good-to-be-true lovers, I wasn’t able to fall into the narrative in its totality.

 

LEFT ON TENTH – by Delia Ephron; directed by Susan Stroman

FEATURING – Julianna Margulies (Delia); Peter Gallagher (Peter); Peter Francis James; and Kate MacCluggage (and Nessa Rose and Charlie).

Scenic design by Beowulf Boritt; costumes by Jeff Mahshie; lighting by Ken Billington and Itohan Edoloyi; sound design by Jill BC Du Boff; projection design by Jeanetter Oi-Suk Yew; wig and hair design by Michael Buonincontro.  At the James Earl Jones Theater: 138 W 48th St, New York, NY 10036.  https://leftontenthbroadway.com/

title.rendered: Meltdown: A Timely and Visionary Play

content.rendered:
Meltdown: A Timely and Visionary Play 

By Edward Kliszus

As election season approaches, Meltdown, the latest production from renowned playwright Toby Armour, makes its timely debut at the Theater for the New City. Running from October 12 to 27, this offbeat fever dream is a must-see for those who crave provocative theater. The play, directed by Joan Kane of Ego Actus Theater Company, blends humor, history, and surrealism. The audience experiences a fresh take on modern-day challenges. Additionally, Armour’s Meltdown explores themes of environmental destruction, climate change, the White House, media outlets, and evolution. Meltdown is an exciting, multidimensional experience. Let’s check out Meltdown: A Timely and Visionary Play.

Debra Khan-Bey (as Ella Fitzgerald) and Peter Dizozza (Composer & Musical Director) in Meltdown at the Theater for the New City. Photo courtesy of production

An All-Star Cast Brings the Characters to Life

The talented cast features the incredible Beth Griffith, Debra Khan-Bey, Holly O’Brien, Mike Roche, and puppeteers Kervin Peralta, Paola Poucel, Nico Negron, and Samantha Sing. Flat puppets and props are by Lytza Colon. Their performances bring Armour’s complex characters to life with humor, heart, and intensity. The main character, Alfie (Mike Roche), delivers a relatable and intense portrayal of a man unraveling in today’s media-obsessed world. With chagrin, rants, and armed with but one vote, he helplessly watches the world’s political chaos through his TV. The richly balanced and sympathetic Janice (Beth Griffith) convinces Alife to doze off to recharge before dinner. Still, his restful dreamscape becomes a series of hallucinations about the past and future. With the help of his new neighbor chanteuse and prognosticator, Sasha (Holly O’Brien), Alfie summons dead presidents and more in his sleep state. He experiences surreal encounters that blend past, present, and future into a dizzying dream of political and social critique. Janice and Sasha’s kindness, patience, and guidance contribute to Alfie’s reawakening and eventual fresh grasp of human nature’s propensities.

Joyous Dance

Moreover, Alfie transforms the frenetic, energetic energy of American Politics into joyous dance routines. One wonders if today’s politics and debate differ from the past and discovers tonight that perhaps a broader view provides sanity or, better yet, peace and tranquility. After all, in 10,000 years, the planet may be covered with oceans, and those left will likely have evolved into some form of sea mammal.

Mike Roche, Holly O’Brien, President Shadow Puppets by Catherine Jane Shaw in a scene from Meltdown at the Theater for the New City. Photo courtesy of production.

Puppets, Lighting, Sound, and Creative Visuals Elevate the Story

What makes Meltdown even more remarkable is its incredibly creative team. Puppet Designer Jane Catherine Shaw brings her exceptional talent to the play, using puppets to guide the audience through Alfie’s fantastical journey. Moreover, the entire production becomes a visual feast with Evan Frank’s innovative set design, Cat Fisher’s striking costumes, and Bruce A! Kraemer’s atmospheric lighting. Peter Dizozza composed the music and performed on piano, using a variety of tonalities and moods to enrich dramatic import. Meikayla Thomany, as production stage manager, coordinated the swirling dervishes of characters, puppets, sound, video, and visual props to craft a flowing potpourri of theatrical elements. The concerted effort of this team undoubtedly brings the play’s themes of environmental disaster and evolution to life in a visceral way. Debra Khan-Bey, as Ella Fitzgerald, delivered delightful song and brought crowd-pleasing joy and gravity to her role.

Mike Roche (as Alfie) and Beth Griffith (as Janice) in a scene from Meltdown at the Theater for the New City. Photo courtesy of production.

The Legacy of Collaboration: Kane and Armour Continue to Innovate

As one might expect, Joan Kane and Toby Armour are no strangers to collaboration. The duo previously worked together on Aunt Susan and her Tennessee Waltz and Freedom Summer—both of which explored untold stories in history, often shedding light on marginalized voices. Consequently, their shared passion for history and socially conscious theater continues with Meltdown. As they tackle the daunting issues of our time, this production marks another successful partnership between Theatre for the New City and Ego Actus Theater Company. In this way, they reinforce their commitment to groundbreaking work rich with integrity and dramatic stagecraft.

Mike Roche (as Aflie) and Holly O’Brien (as Sasha) in a scene from Meltdown at the Theater for the New City. Courtesy of Production

A Timely Message Delivered During Election Season

Bruce A! Kraemer, producer of Ego Actus, enthusiastically shared his thoughts on the perfect timing of this production: “Meltdown has a crazy take on history, climate change, immigration, and so much more. Producing Meltdown during election season is the perfect time to stage this story.” Indeed, the timing of this premiere couldn’t be more appropriate. As the world grapples with ongoing environmental disasters, social unrest, and political turmoil, Meltdown captures the current mood of uncertainty and change.

The cast of Meltdown at the Theater for the New City. L-R: Mike Roche, Beth Griffith, Holly O’Brien, and Debra Khan-Bey (top row). Kervin Peralta, Paola Poucel, Nico Negron, and Samantha Sing (bottom row). Photo courtesy of production.

Meltdown: A Timely and Visionary Play

By Toby Armour and Directed by Joan Kane

Theater For the New City

155 First Ave. (at E. 10th Street)
New York NY
Box office (212) 254-1109, www.theaterforthenewcity.net

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Gidion’s Knot , written by Johnna Adams, places us into a fifth-grade classroom, maybe it’s midday; we hear a bell, we hear laughter, we wait over an hour for a principal that will never show. But a child’s mother, Suzanne Di Donna, —a parent whose son has died—does show for her son’s parent-teacher conference–a parent who not only shows because it was a scheduled appointment but because she is yearning for answers. Maybe her grief hasn’t set in yet—maybe the skepticism of the circumstances has just surfaced.

Gidion’s Knot puts the way teachers and parents navigate communication and professionalism on stage. The gaps, the silences, create the tense space where we sit, surrounding these two adults on two very opposite sides of tragedy, as they navigate each other’s emotions.

Kirsten Russell, Gidion’s teacher, shows us the poise an educator wrestles to maintain in tragedy, their vulnerability and hesitation. As Gidion’s story unfolds, we understand more and more of his intentions and potential motives, as both his mother and teacher struggle to allow themselves to understand each other.

An anxiety-ridden, awkward conference turns into an argument of children’s innocence.

We’re asked whether childhood is a state of innocence or if it should rather be a state of losing innocence. We experience the responsibility to protect children. How what we speak and do influences them, their naivety, their vulnerability.

When it comes to the imagination of a child, can–should–teachers tell students what not to write about? How much influence should we hold over the stories they choose to tell, those they rehash, or imagine? Perhaps, we should be digging into their motivation for their work and presentation, the rationality behind how they conduct themselves. Gidion’s Knot is effective in the way we come to understand the young children involved in tragedy.

As an educator, it is a constant endeavor of finding the balance between confident and authority, the gray area of disclosure of self, disclosure of students to their own parents, preserving honesty and integrity. Balancing affection and concern with excitement and fervor. Refraining from casting our judgements and opinions, the poise we maintain in stressful and testing environments.

Gidion’s Knot reminds us of the importance to maintaining a supportive and safe environment. This performance allows the audience to meet these two women–and maybe we are already silently judging as each one enters the space; or as details pertaining to the circumstances are slowly released. We discover more about Gidion’s background, home life, and social life as we grow annoyed along with Gidion’s mother and uncomfortable with Gidion’s teacher, waiting for their principal to arrive.

This performance sets the stage for the external factors that affect students. Gidion’s Knot takes us through several surprising and dismantling twists. The story, along with Suzanne Di Donna and Kirsten Russell, are strong, fierce, and brave as we are dropped into Gidion’s unsettling young life.

“It was my responsibility. I’m sure you understand. I’m sure you understand now.”

 

Written by Johnna Adams; Produced by Talya Dayan; Directed by Rich Pecci.

CAST: Suzanne Di Donna (Gidion’s Mother), Kirsten Russell (teacher).

CREATIVE TEAM: Mark Wendland (Scenic Design), Jess Goldstein (Costume Design), Japhy Weidman (Lighting Design), Dan Moses Schreier (Original Music and Sound Design), Lucy Mackinnon (Projection Design), Tom Schall (Fight Direction), Charles G. LPointe (Hair and Wig Design), Ashley Ryan (makeup Design), and Charlotte Fleck (Dialect Coach).

Gidion’s Knot, will play at The Flea Theater, 20 Thomas St. (between Broadway & Church St., in Tribeca, New York, NY on Saturdays, Oct. 26 and Nov. 2 at 8:30PM. Tickets can be purchased here.

This full length play is part of the Circle Theater Festival. Full length plays at the Circle Theater Festival will show throughout the day on Saturday Oct. 26 and Nov. 2, and several one-act plays will show in productions of three one-acts on Saturday Oct. 26 and Nov. 2 as well at The Flea Theater.

CREATIVE TEAM: Emma Tadmor (Artistic Director), Talya Dayan (Creative Producer), Victoria Kempter (PR & Sponsorship Director), Julianne Mason (Sound Designer), Elijah Kleinberg (Lighting Designer).

By Sarah Downs

I had a hot date on Saturday night with, of all people, Franz Kafka!  Who knew one of the world’s more depressed icons of 20th century literature could be so much fun?  Kafkaesque! currently playing at Theatre 154 celebrates the laugh riot that is Kafka’s oevre, particularly his finest creation, Gregor Samsa.  In an amazing feat of alchemy (Kafka would approve), James Harvey lampoons Kafka’s writing while maintaining its heart.

From start to finish Kafkaesque! is engaging, funny and even a little soulful.  It’s so good that when the show drew to a close I wondered where the time went.  The cast is uniformly excellent.  They sing, dance and handle comedy with equal finesse.  Josh Nasser, in the role of QAnon-adjacent patriarch Michael Samsa, has a powerful voice and easy presence.  In his plaid shirt and aging trucker hat Michael is the picture of bewildered bro-culture, drowning in failed capitalist angst.  As his fresh faced wife Karen, Emily Olcott sparkles, with a iron determination and a sweet smile plastered on her face even as Karen’s fate seems increasingly dim.  Olcott also plays quite affectingly an undercurrent of vulnerability beneath the comedy.  Their girly, Gen Z daughter Greta (Alexandra Nader) earphones permanently attached to her head, bursts with youngest child energy.  Greta’s ambition to ‘win’ at social media makes her the most tuned in member of her family (ironically).  Nader lights up the stage in a performance that reaches right out to the audience and invites us into her party.

And of course there’s  our hero.  Gregor, with his newly acquired wings and bug eyes, pulling at our heartstrings as he fights existential ennui.  As if working a menial job weren’t bad enough, now Gregor has six legs and antennae to contend with.  Curry Whitmire, with easy physical comedy and mobile facial expressions,  is utterly charming as the earnest, hapless innocent.

Director Ashley Brooke Monroe.keeps the show humming at just the right pace.  She doesn’t rush the laughs, leans into the satire, and draws clear stage pictures that offer the most information with a minimum of fuss.  Similarly the choreography hits the sweet spot where dancing is an extension of movement.  It’s not ‘stagey.’  The actors wear their characters like a comfortable suit of clothes. The comedy may move across the footlights but not in a way that would make either performers or audience feel self-conscious..  Even the set changes in this simple, playing space go smoothly.  Indeed, the spare set and ‘cabaret’ style setup are perfect for this piece.  We don’t need clutter.  The richness of a simple red curtain, which Bentley Hyedt’s lighting transforms into a plush velvet drama queen, and two mismatched vintage chandeliers say “luxury” while the lamp-lit café tables with cockroach embossed lampshades say “absurdity.”  Is it possible we’re at the …Café Kaf-kyle?

Harvey’s witty, tuneful songs flow with timely reference and welcome irreverence – and they’re smart.  We happily follow the material wherever it goes.  Even the drudgery of bureaucracy is played for laughs.  And there are so many.  From start to finish Kafkaesque! is – dare I say it?  Adorable.  You know that feeling when you leave a performance with a smile on your face and the final song still playing in your head.  Or perhaps it was just successful cognitive behavioral therapy, as I do have a horror of cockroaches.  Whatevs.  This show treated me to some of the funniest 90 minutes I’ve experienced in a long, long time.  What can I say?  It is truly a transformational experience…

Kafkaesque! written by James Harvey and directed by Ashley Brooke Monroe.

With James Harvey  as Franz Kafka, Alexandra Nader as Greta, Josh Nasser as Michael, Emily Olcott as Karen/Josephine, and Curry Whitmire as Gregor.

Choreography by Sara Gibbons, set design by Taylor Friel, costume design by Maggie Walsh  and lighting design buy Bentley Heydt.  Produced by Patrick Trettenero and Staro Industries.

At Theatre 154 (formerly the New Ohio Theatre) through November 10th.  Tickets HERE or go to www.ootbtheatrics.com.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Margret Echeverria

Hey, You; crying in your martini about a particular Tuesday in November: This is New York City; home of some of the yummiest drag queens in the world.  Pay your tab and head on over to New World Stages for DRAG The Musical where the problems are solvable, the songs come from stellar pipes in very hot costumes and the camp dial is set as high as the wigs!

Queens rule and their subjects are peaceful when jurisdictions are agreed upon, but when bitches get their hearts broken, power grabs for territory can erupt in feuds of fierceness.  We have two fabulous drag clubs across the street from one another – The Fish Tank and The Cat House – owned and operated by House Mothers, Alexis Gillmore (Nick Adams) and Kitty Galloway (Alaska Thunderfuck), respectively, who used to be two  drag artists in love; one classic and one modern.  Now, they are feeding a war between them in a puritanical culture bred in a punishing economy.  Adams exudes an energy reminiscent of Mitchell’s Hedwig with a smile bigger than her biceps (and that’s saying something) hiding an aching heart.  Thunderfuck smolders as Kitty giving Crawford vibes in costumes to die for.

The music shakes the house with beats that will have you forget these two hours have no intermission.  Tuna Turner (LaGoona Bloo) has the legs that deserve her character’s namesake and they are only outdone by her expansive vocal range.  Puss Puss DuBois (Nick Laughlin) is the shy girl at the slumber party, whose naiveté, Southern accent and diminutive stature are as endearing as her full facial beard.  But where Puss Puss’ dance steps falter, Laughlin, a professional

Jan Sport, Jujubee, Nick Laughlin and Alaska Thunderfuck in DRAG_The Musical. Photo by Matthew Murphy

choreographer, sings your socks off.  Dixie Coxworth (Liisi LaFontaine) brings freshness to this story as a cis gender female drag queen – yasssss, Girl; bring it up to 2024! – and her acting skills are polished, working real moments that land nicely into this romp.  Savannah St. James (Jan Sport) and The Tigress (JuJuBee) bring sweet voluptuousness to the stage that matches their vocal stylings curling through your ear and also curling this plump former opera student’s lips into a grateful smile.

I am pleased to report that the story falls just shy of lost to the gags, glam and glory; we find out why Alexis was hurt by her family before she ever met Kitty when we meet her brother, Tom Hutchinson (Joey McIntyre), coming to rescue The Fish Tank from financial ruin with a heavy dose of guilt that melts into love and understanding.  McIntyre is one of those performers who is having a great time on the stage always inspiring us to do happy wiggles in our seats.  And there is an awesome kid in this cast:  Brendan Hutchinson, played by Yair Keydar in the show I saw, who made me cry with a performance so evocative of those painful pre-pubescent years we all experienced whether we questioned our sexuality or not.

Drunk Jerry (Eddie Korbich) is that one friend you kick yourself for enabling.  Korbich steals every scene with wonderful mischief that reminds me of many late nights in the ‘90’s club scene when I laughed so hard I needed to carry albuterol in my handbag.  Good laughs come from deep pain and it is Drunk Jerry who eventually sobers all his friends.

The powerhouse performances of Alaska Thunderfuck and Nick Adams could have overwhelmed this show, but these are gracious monarchs who allow others to shine and the message to be felt: Our humanity, our connection to one another and our relentless pursuit of the next fun way to do the next right thing will not be defeated by any rabid prejudice disguising itself as greedy oligarchs or government tax collectors because there will always be those who save the world by just being love in DRAG.  Sing it, Sisters!

DRAG THE MUSICAL – Book, Music, and Lyrics by Tomas Costanza, Justin Andrew Honard and Ashley Gordon

WITH Lagoona Bloo (Tuna Turner), Luxx Noir London (Popcorn), Liisi La Fontaine (Dixie Coxworth), Nick Adams (Alexis Gillmore), Jan Sport (Savannah St. James), Jujubee (The Tigress), Nick Laughlin (Puss Puss DuBois), Alaska Thunderfuck (Kitty Galloway), Joey McIntyre (Tom Hutchinson), Yair Keydar/Remi Tuckman (Brendan Hutchinson), Eddie Korbich (Drunk Jerry), J. Elaine Marcos (Gloria Schmidt/Rita Laritz/Liberty Van Der Snatch; Ensemble:  Nicholas Kraft, Christine Shepard, Kodiak Thompson, Teddy Wilson Jr.

Scenic design, Jason Sherwood; Costume design, Marco Marco; Lighting design,  Adam Honore; Sound design, Drew Levy; Projection design, Aaron Rhyne; Makeup design, Aurora Sexton

Through November 11, 2025 at New World Stages, 340 West 50th Street.  Get tickets here.

Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

How do you define ‘trauma?’  Is it Pain?  Fear?  Desperation?  Doubt?  For the characters In Ashes & Ink it’s all of that and more.  Molly (Kathryn Erbe), her son Quinn (Julian Shatkin) and her boyfriend Leo (Javier Molina) wrestle with the undercurrent of their individual traumas, which threaten to drown them at every turn.

The death of Molly’s husband has thrown her life into turmoil, as she struggles to survive, both emotionally and financially.  For Quinn, the trauma of his father’s death is deeply personal and catastrophically public, as he has fallen into the trap of addiction.   Several stints in rehab have led to repeated escape and relapse.  Not only can he not pull himself free, it is not clear that he wants to.  Death also haunts Leo and his son Felix (Rhylee Watson).   After the loss of his wife, Leo has moved Felix and himself out of the city, intent on starting a new life.  The problem is, no matter where you go, there you are.  Emotional baggage is the only baggage that never gets lost in transit.

Ashes & Ink seeks to illuminate the isolation of grief and how individual struggles can intertwine and poison relationships.  It’s as if everyone is crying in the wilderness, but no-one is listening.  People fight shadows.  Unfortunately, this shadow boxing applies to the actors as well as their characters, as the actors have to fight the material to create an overall emotional arc.  Best intentions notwithstanding, the play falls a little flat.  The performance has seemingly only two speeds  –  low, almost inaudible energy or high drama, with little to no  transition between the two.  Marha Pichey’s writing is inconsistent as well.  Some of the dialogue is too on the nose, although there are some moments of beauty, particulary in monologue.

The structure of many small scenes that alternate between two distinct locations, Molly’s apartment and Leo’s home, necessitates frequent interruptions as the actors change the set.  Bouncing between places, they are forced to break the action just when things get going, reset, and then rush to conjure drama out of thin air before they have to stop and do it all over again.  The constant lights up/lights down is a bit destabilizing.  In fairness, however, I can’t fully assess the potential for these transitions to feel more seamless, as the production is clearly just getting on its feet.  I’m sure as the run continues, there will be fewer awkward bumps in the road.

Similarly, while the actors are excellent, their performances are a bit uneven.  Individual textures clash. Kathryn Erbe underplays as Molly and Javier Molina nearly turns somersaults trying to inject some romance into their relationship.  I’m sorry to say this but while pleasant together, Erbe and Molina don’t have any real chemistry.  That is perhaps intentional, as all of Molly’s attention is understandably wrapped up in trying to heal her relationship with her son Quinn.  I appreciate that in her quietness, Erbe does not rush her work.  She is willing to wait for a moment to happen.  By contrast, Julian Shatkin as Quinn, fighting his battle with addiction, is understandably overwrought.  However, his outsize, angry young man energy is such it feels a bit as if he’s in a different play.  As Molly’s sister Bree, Tamara Flannagan has a nice quality, but she is given nothing to work with.  In all of the hurly-burly, a child could easily get lost, but Rhylee Watson as sweet Felix holds his own.  In some ways, Felix is a fulcrum in the drama.  Perhaps it is his innocence, but everyone is drawn to him.

The set itself is beautiful.  Tim McMath has cleverly created one static, detailed unit and one large mobile unit which effects the toggle between the Molly’s office and Leo’s home.  It is a large set change, but with minimal fuss.  I do get the sense that the design has been abbreviated in order to fit in the small space at AMT.  That may explain why Molly’s office is complete in every detail, whereas Leo’s home is more of a sketch.  The focus is certainly geared that way.   Paul Hudson’s seamless lighting design moves from the warmly lit coziness of Molly’s office to the more challenging task of delineating Leo’s cooler, minimal world.  The design’s beauty, however, comes to its true fruition during the set changes.  Dark violets and greens of night time enfold us, as shadows of leaves ripple on the walls, as if gently moving on the breeze. The birdsong that could arguably be considered a fifth character in the play, intensifies, creating a near hypnotic effect.  It feels like a reward.  If they could bottle that and sell it, self-help apps would go out of business.\

Ashes & Ink, by Martha Pichey.  Directed by Alice Jankell.

With Kathryn Erbe, Julian Shatkin, Javier Molina, Tamara Flannagan and Rhylee Watson.

Set design by Tim McMath, lighting design by Paul Hudson, costume design by Kaitlin Feinberg, sound design by Alex Attalla.

At AMT (354 West 54th St., NYC) through November 3rd.  Tickets HERE or go to www.AMTtheater.org.  Runtime 90 minutes with no intermission.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Victoria Weisfeld

The current production of Macbeth at The Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey, directed by Brian B. Crowe, is the sort of don’t-miss production that represents theater at its best (October 19  through November 17). Macbeth was the first STNJ production we saw, many years ago, and we’ve been coming back ever since. The current production may have the same effect on you. STNJ has picked the right season for it, note the witches, and “ambition, power, and madness” are not unfamiliar to us nearly 420 years later.

In the hands of this cast and director, the familiar story is freshly experienced and builds to an immensely powerful effect: the eerie muttering of Banquo’s ghost; Macduff’s heart-rending breakdown at news of his family’s murder (I needed some minutes to recover); Malcolm’s tears at his father’s death; Lady Macbeth’s piteous descent into madness; the climactic sword-clashing fight between Macbeth and Macduff; and the strong performance of Ray Fisher, whose masculinity embodies Macbeth’s successes and crumbles before you—all elevate the ancient story into the realm of timeless emotion. The witches’ gestures, choreography, costumes, and choral effects are especially noteworthy.

You know the story. Successful Scottish general Macbeth (played by Ray Fisher), in company with fellow general Banquo (R.J. Foster) is returning to Macbeth’s home, Dunsinane Castle. They encounter three witches (Ellie Gossage, Aurea Tomeski, and Felix Mayes) who predict Macbeth will become Thane of Cawdor and king of Scotland and Banquo will be the father of kings. Before Macbeth can even reach home, two noblemen (Dino Curia and Nathan Flesh) confirm he’s been named Cawdor.

Macbeth tells his wife (Erin Partin) about the predictions, and they devise a shortcut to achieving them. While King Duncan (Earl Baker, Jr.) sleeps, Macbeth murders him. The next morning, Scottish noblemen Lennox (Jordan Laroya) and Macduff (Clark Carmichael) discover the murder.

As King, Macbeth is tormented by the deed that gained him the crown and the further murders necessary to keep it, including those of Macduff’s wife and children. Gradually, he and Lady Macbeth descend into madness and paranoia.

He seeks out the witches, who conjure spirits whose prophecies suggest to him he’s invincible. A force led by the vengeance-seeking Macduff and Prince Malcolm (Gerrard James) prove him wrong.

Aspects of this story clearly touch on themes Shakespeare returned to again and again. Think upon “uneasy lies the head that wears a crown” (Henry IV, Part 2) and “conscience doth make cowards of us all” (Hamlet).

The simple, almost brutal set accommodates the play’s many scenes, the costumes are sumptuous, and the creative team has developed a succession of deft touches that intensify the experience.

Production credits to Brian Ruggaber (set design), Andrew Hungerford (lighting design), Melanie Chen Cole (sound design), Rodrigo Muñoz (costumes), and Doug West (fight director).

STNJ productions are hosted at Drew University in Madison, N.J. (easily reachable from NYC by train). For tickets, call the box office at 973-408-5600 or visit the Box Office online.

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Get Ready for DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead—and a Few Eyebrows

If you’re looking for an experience that will scare you, seduce you, and make you laugh harder than you have in ages, then Jonny Porkpie’s DEAD SEXY is your ticket to a delightfully devilish night out. This twisted tale of titillation and terror has clawed its way back from the grave for a limited run at the Laurie Beechman Theatre, just in time for Halloween. So, if you’re in the mood for a bit of mischief, a little mayhem, and some classic Burlesque entertainment, strap in —because DEAD SEXY promises to be the wildest, weirdest, and deliciously naughty show you’ll see this season. Gear up for DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead.

Cheeky Humor

With its unique fusion of horror, burlesque, and cheeky humor, DEAD SEXY has already garnered a cult following. After selling out its Off-Broadway runs in 2015 and 2016, the show is back from the dead for three performances, each more seductive and spine-chilling than the last. Part striptease, part vaudeville, part horror-comedy—DEAD SEXY is what happens when you mix the sensual art of burlesque with the campy theatrics of a B-movie horror flick like Role of the Vampire, Bloody Pit of Horror or the Awful Dr. Orlof. And it’s every bit as outrageous as it sounds.

Jonny Porkpie on stage in a scene from DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead. Photo by Don Spiro

A Sinister Plot: Science, Seduction, and a Dash of the Macabre

At the center of this creepy cabaret is Doctor’s Evil Laboratory & Cabaret, a setting where science and seduction intertwine in the most unexpected and naughtiest ways. The plot is as devilishly absurd as it is deliciously fun: a mad scientist, his aberrant assistant, and a seductive intern are on a mission to revive a dearly departed lover from the underworld. But they don’t rely on your average resurrection rituals—oh no, these twisted geniuses use the power of Vaudvillian Burlesque to bring the dead back to life.

It’s a night of flirty fiends and glamorous ghouls, where the dead don’t stay dead for long, and each act pushes the boundaries of what can and should be on stage. The plot, if we can even call it that, is more of a framework for the show’s main attraction: a series of outrageous, laugh-out-loud, funny burlesque performances that blend the grotesque with the glamorous along with absurd interviews and comedic references to iPhones, electric cars, and the presidential election.

High Camp  Meets Lingerie

You’ll see everything from sinister striptease that sends chills down your spine to the mad scientist’s macabre love story that is as twisted as it’s tantalizing. Imagine an unhinged scientist reanimating the dead he killed to perform in his burlesque show on 42nd Street—then imagine what happens when the dead can’t help but undress. It’s a night where high camp meets lingerie, and the result is a theatrical spectacle that will leave you howling—sometimes in mock fear, but mostly from laughter. The audience began laughing and clapping at the first gibe and didn’t stop until it was over.

The Cast: Killer Talent, Undead Appeal

The success of DEAD SEXY lies in its inventive premise and the stellar cast of burlesque stars who make the undead look drop-dead gorgeous. Jonny Porkpie, the show’s creator and star, plays the master of ceremonies and sinister scientist. Known as the “Burlesque Mayor of New York City,” Porkpie has spent years perfecting the art of burlesque comedy, and his performance in DEAD SEXY is the perfect combination of witty and risqué. His jokes are as sharp as his attire is irreverent, and his timing is impeccable—making him the ideal guide through this weird and wonderful world of undead iniquity. His assistant and foil, Tigger (with his mysteriously suspicious Dr. Frankenstein German accent), continually interrupts to ensure each experiment ends with a burlesque performance.

Unique Flair

Some of the most talented performers in the burlesque scene join him on stage, including Jo Weldon, Syn Sultress (who turns out to be a spy for the organization funding the sinister scientist’s experiments), and Tigger as his lab assistant Teegor (pronounced Igor)! These performers bring a mix of glamour, talent, and pure, unadulterated sex appeal and fun to the show. Special guest appearances are peppered throughout the run, with Peekaboo Pointe performing on October 12 and 19, Mr. Gorgeous showing off his considerable talents on October 19, and the tantalizing Maine Attraction closing the season on October 26. Each performer brings their unique flair to the stage, whether Peekaboo Pointe’s classic striptease skills, Mr. Gorgeous’s dashing good looks, acrobatic feats, Frankenstein monster monolithic monologue interview, or The Maine Attraction’s powerful stage presence.

A Dash of Vaudeville – DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead

Together, this killer cast delivers a series of equally shocking, hilarious, and undeniably seductive performances. You won’t just be watching performers relive the golden days of burlesque with a dash of vaudeville—you’ll be witnessing a masterclass in how burlesque can entertain, provoke, and evoke humor.

Jonny Porkpie and Jo Weldon in a scene from DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead. Photo by Don Spiro

The Art of Tease (and Terror): Why Burlesque and Horror Go Hand in Hand

At first glance, burlesque and horror might seem like strange bedfellows (though DEAD SEXY makes a strong case for why they should be), but the truth is these two genres share much common ground. Both rely on suspense, aim to push boundaries, and often play with taboos and social conventions. In burlesque, the performer teases the audience, building anticipation before finally revealing their body with carefully placed pasties, twirling tassel dervishes, and lingerie; in horror, the filmmaker teases the viewer, building tension before delivering the scare.

Tease and Terror

In DEAD SEXY, this relationship between tease and terror is pushed to its limits. Each act studies how to keep the audience on the edge of their seats through a dance performance or a comedic interview. And because this is burlesque, the focus is always on seduction—even when the performers play undead ghouls.

The genius of DEAD SEXY lies in its ability to blend these two genres seamlessly. The horror elements never overshadow the parody, and the burlesque never feels out of place in the horror setting. Instead, the two genres complement each other, creating a show greater than the sum of its parts. It’s a night of thrilling burlesque and chilling humor, where the scares are just as satisfying as the burlesque.

Jonny Porkpie: The Man Behind the Madness

At the heart of DEAD SEXY is Jonny Porkpie, the mastermind behind the show and the “Burlesque Mayor of New York City.” Porkpie is a veteran of the burlesque scene, having produced and emceed countless shows over the years, including his internationally acclaimed burlesque gameshow, The Nayked Truth, which toured 30 cities in five countries. He’s also the founder of Pinchbottom Burlesque, which was named the best burlesque in NYC by both New York Magazine and The Village Voice.

Porkpie’s sense of humor sets DEAD SEXY apart from other burlesque shows. His jokes are clever, often full of double entendres and playful wordplay that keeps the audience laughing long after the act has ended. And yet, Porkpie is just as comfortable playing with the show’s darker elements, injecting just the right amount of comedic horror into each performance to keep the audience on their toes.

His ability to blend humor, horror, and seduction into one cohesive show makes DEAD SEXY unique. It’s a rare talent to make audiences laugh, gasp, and blush in the same breath, but Porkpie easily pulls it off.

Jo Weldon in a scene from Jonny Porkpie and Jo Weldon in a scene from DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead. Photo by Don Spiro

What to Expect: A Night of Naughty Fun (with a Side of Screams)

So, what can you expect when you step into the Laurie Beechman Theatre for DEAD SEXY? First, they have a great dining menu and drinks, comfortable seating, and excellent service. Most of all, be prepared for a lot of laughs and fun. The show is as much a comedy as a burlesque revue, and the performers aren’t afraid to ham it up on stage (rim shot humor without the drums!). In addition to cast members roaming and interacting with the audience, to the crowd’s delight, three brave audience members joined in the fun on stage when I attended. Expect plenty of puns, jokes, and innuendos that will leave you chuckling long after the curtain has fallen.

Of course, this is burlesque, so expect some skin. The performers may be playing undead characters, but they’re still as seductive as spooky. And while the striptease acts are undoubtedly spicy, they’re also incredibly inventive. When was the last time you saw talent-driven spinning tassels? Perhaps you remember Elvira, Mistress of the Dark? But at DEAD SEXY, you won’t just see traditional burlesque—you’ll see horror-themed performances that are as creative as they are titillating.

Hilarious

But don’t forget the horror! This is still a Halloween show, and plenty of spooky moments are sprinkled throughout. Whether it’s a blood-curdling scream, a surprise scare, or a gory (but hilarious) demise, DEAD SEXY knows how to keep the audience on the edge of their seat. And because the show blends horror and comedy so well, these moments are never too scary—they’re just scary enough to keep you guessing.

One thing’s sure: by the night’s end, you’ll be left breathless—not just from the scares.

Why DEAD SEXY is the Perfect Halloween Treat – DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead

Halloween is all about celebrating the macabre, the mysterious, and the strange, and there’s no better way to do that than with a night of burlesque horror. DEAD SEXY offers a unique twist on the usual Halloween fare, combining the thrills of a B-rated horror movie with the sensuality of a burlesque show. It’s a night where anything can happen—and usually does.

If you’re looking for something different to do this Halloween season, DEAD SEXY is the perfect choice. Whether you’re a burlesque fan, a horror lover, or just someone looking for a good laugh, this show has something for everyone. It’s a sexy, spooky, and downright hilarious night of entertainment that will leave you begging for more.

Maine Attraction in a scene from DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead. Photo by Don Spiro. Photo by Don Spiro

Dead Sexy at the Laurie Beechman Theatre

Final Thoughts: DEAD SEXY Is to Die For

There’s no denying that DEAD SEXY is one of the most unique shows you’ll see this Halloween season. Its burlesque, horror, and comedy blend offers a little something for everyone. Whether you come for the scares, the laughs, or the dancers, you’ll leave thoroughly entertained.

Sounds, lighting, costumes, and multi-media visuals were excellent!

But don’t just take my word for it. Head down to the Laurie Beechman Theatre and see why DEAD SEXY has become a cult favorite.

Performances run on October 12 and 19 at 7 p.m. and October 26 at 9:30 p.m. Tickets are available at SpinCycleNYC.com, and you’ll want to grab them before they’re gone—after all, nothing stays dead forever.

A publicity poster for DEAD SEXY: The Burlesque Thriller That’ll Raise the Dead. Photo by Don Spiro. Photo by Don Spiro

Review by Brittany Crowell

Benjamin Franklin, famous inventor, statesman, dreamer, publisher, scientist, and … father?  Franklinland at Ensemble Studio Theater explores the relationship between the Franklin we’ve all heard of and his son, William Franklin, who was a politician and loyalist and lived his later years in exile in the United Kingdom.  Lloyd Suh (playwright) looks at the relationship between these two different individuals and how this may have driven them down such different paths.  

In Franklinland, we find father Franklin to be charmingly pompous and self-assured while young Franklin Jr fights for the right to be released from his father’s tight grip and high aspirations.  Franklinland itself is Benjamin’s term for Nova Scotia, an island off the coast which he intended to use as a land for his experiments and imaginings.  Suh takes the perspective that Franklin deprioritizes his work on this land, intending instead to make the new USA his experiment, much to his son’s chagrin.

Cheeky and fun, the script maps a wonderful collaboration between the dialogue of 18th century colonies and modern speak.  It’s peppered with moments of “what? / what? / what? / never-mind” in which father and son cross wires and continue to misunderstand each other.  The play takes us from young apprentice William through to his final meeting with his father in his London exile.  Suh plays well with the history and the audience will find themselves enjoying moments of historical recognition paralleling an education in this famous father-son relationship.  However, the script somehow seemed to stumble in its journey from page to stage. What should feel like an enticing paternal tug-of-war falls flat and the audience is left with more of an historical lesson than an emotional and cathartic journey.  

Perhaps the chemistry was off in the performance that I saw; there was a lack of ease in the blocking (by director Chika Ike) and the piece was missing the smoothness needed for the audience to truly settle in and be taken on a journey.  Thomas Jay Ryan is quite convincing as Benjamin Franklin and it’s clear that he’s having a blast in the role, but perhaps a little too much as there were moments where he himself began to chuckle while the audience wasn’t in on the joke. Noah Keyishian journeys from timid to proud as William Franklin and while his performance is endearing and sympathetic, I’m hopeful that he will settle even further into the role as the run continues.  Mason Reeves makes a quick appearance in the final scene of the play as William Jr and brings a fresh energy to the scene, as well as some hope for the future of the Franklins and a reconciliation amongst the generations.

The scenic design by Riw Rakkulchon, with properties designed by Thomas Jenkeleit, builds a beautiful tapestry of experimentation and imagination.  Papers and research pepper the wooden cabin-esque walls and there are walls muttered with tools and others of disassembled chairs. Costumes by Christopher Vergara create a picture of Franklin as we know him. Lighting designer Carolina Ortiz Herrera plays with the flickering candles on the walls, creates lightning through the paned window, and an other-worldly blue glow seeps through the wooded cabin panels to bring us from scene to scene (complimented by sound and original compositions by Daniela Hart, Bailey  Trierweiler, Noel Nichols, and UptownWorks).

Overall the piece is enjoyable, but not as strong as it would be with either a little more rehearsal, a snappier pace, and/or better chemistry between performers.  As it stands, it’s a wonderful look into this historical father-son relationship in a fun and quirky setting.

 

FRANKLINLAND – by Lloyd Suh; directed by Chika Ike

FEATURING:  Thomas Jay Ryan (Benjamin Franklin); Noah Keyishian (William Franklin); and Mason Reeves (William Temple Franklin)

Scenic design by Riw Rakkulchon; costumes by Christopher Vergara; lighting by Carolina Ortiz Herrara; properties design, Thomas Jenkeleit; sound and original compositions by Daniela Hart, Bailey Trierweiler, Noel Nichols, and Uptown Works.  Presented by Ensemble Studio Theater: Estefania Fadul and Graeme Gillis, co-artistic directors.  Through November 3.  545 West 52nd Street. www.ensemblestudiotheatre.org/20242025/2024/6/franklinland

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“A new century. A new millennium.”

Fast forward to election night of Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin’s second term.

We hear Putin’s speech in Russian playing on the television, a speech that has aired hours prior.

Vladimir’s cast of several incredible actors that double in roles, presents us with Raya (Francesca Faridany), a Russian news journalist and author, and Kostya (Norbert Leo Butz), her boss, who leads the Moscow Novosti, a Russian news outlet. Intense moments of Raya and Kostya cross their personal and professional relationship while they navigate the boundaries of reporting, and questions of morality and commitment that come with this profession in media.

Simultaneously, Raya’s career creates anxiety and concern for her daughter, Galina (Olivia Deren Nikkanen). And to make a balance of career, family, and mental and physical health even more challenging, Galina is engaged; a wedding needs to be planned.

As this piece immediately places the reader into a significant time in Russian power changes and influx, it would most benefit the audience if they arrive with a knowledge of Putin’s rise as president and prime minister and Russia’s role in the Second Chechnyan War. Without this understanding, the play almost solely embodies the risk journalists take in war zones and when exposing hidden information—and the danger they bring onto those involved in their investigations and conversations. Journalists are essentially reporting on power—a significant part of any war.

Raya is turned onto a complaint from an American investor about someone that used his company to claim for a very large tax refund, which ended up getting paid to the company: the largest tax refund in American history. Someone at the top of the Russian government was getting a cut, and Raya decided to take on the story independently.

Vladimir drops us into memories, or dream-like scenes, of Raya finding individuals that can help her expose the Russian government—but equally expose their own identities. Chovka (Erin Darke), a woman in Raya’s dreams, questions morals and intentions of reporters, while also questioning the mindsets of victims of their own countries.

During one conversation, Chovka says, “…I lost my heart.” We empathize with the hopelessness that Russians have adopted, and whether it is good.

Photo Credit, Jeremy Daniel

The betrayal of one’s country is examined—whether journalists are betraying their country by bringing the evil, the disturbing, the ugly to light. Within the government stands the state run media outlets; we consider how and when a news outlet releases information to the public. When Raya is suddenly, unexpectedly at risk, we later learn that a source may had already reported this—but Raya, the victim, was not informed. In larger explosions and incidents, like the Beslan School Siege—where over 300 people died (but that’s just what news reported)—we wonder how many lives could have been saved if state-run news would have rather been an independently run source rleeasing information. The level to which a government can contain and manipulate information.

Numerous directions of morality and betrayal are questioned. Is a public debate democracy or theater? Are “good” journalists shit stirrers?—those that are willing to put their lives at risk to tell the stories of those directly suffering or affected by a war, a government?

Are talks about Russian government really different from that of other countries?

Ultimately, we leave the theater thinking of the reasons journalists risk themselves and even others for the truth. “The only reason I’m still doing this, the only reason, is because no one else is.”

Despite the danger to which Raya, and other “good” journalists are exposed, they seem to return to their country time and time again.

“It’s where I’m useful.”

“It’s worth it.”

“It’s my home.”

Photo Credit, Jeremy Daniel

Vladimir, Written by Erika Sheffer; Directed by Daniel Sullivan.

CAST: Norbert Leo Butz (Kostya), Erin Darke (Chovka & Others), Francesca Faridany (Raya), Erik Jensen (Andrei & Others), Olivia Deren Nikkanen (Galina & Others), David Rosenberg (Yevgeny), and Jonathan Walker (Jim & Others).

CREATIVE TEAM: Mark Wendland (Scenic Design), Jess Goldstein (Costume Design), Japhy Weidman (Lighting Design), Dan Moses Schreier (Original Music and Sound Design), Lucy Mackinnon (Projection Design), Tom Schall (Fight Direction), Charles G. LPointe (Hair and Wig Design), Ashley Ryan (makeup Design), and Charlotte Fleck (Dialect Coach).

Running time is 2 hours and 15 minutes, including one 10 minute intermission.

Vladimir, will play at Manhattan Theatre Club, New York City Center Stage I, 131 West 55th Street, until November 10, 2024. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Very few works in the English language can credibly be described as timeless, but none is more deserving of the term than Thornton Wilder’s 1938 lesson on life, Our Town. It is a play about many things, indeed it is a play about everything, but the movement of time itself is this Pulitzer-winning drama’s top concern, calling out our failure to appreciate life as it speeds by, and our stubborn inability to cope when the book of days inevitably slams shut.

Wilder wrote with such clarity, authority and wisdom that his words refuse to grow stale. They resist the need for scenery and deep characterization, making Our Town an actor-proof work that is as effective at the smallest of community theaters as it is on Broadway. Given its universal themes, the play is also resistant to reinterpretation, but in this new and densely populated staging at the Barrymore Theatre, director Kenny Leon gives it his best shot.

Time and place are unmoored in Our Town and Leon lands his 28 member multiracial cast down in a 1901 version of Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire that is futuristic in its inclusiveness; a world that is a wish, where interracial romance is de rigueur and every citizen is fluent in sign language. There is also musicality. As the cast assembles, Abraham Jam’s  “Braided Prayer” is played. It is a spiritual melody that weaves together Muslim, Jewish and Christian invocations, bringing Hebrew to New Hampshire. The song sets a tone that does not especially sync with the rest of the evening, though it strikes a chord whenever the play reaches back into the biblical realm, as when we are reminded, “Babylon once had two million people in it, and all we know about ’em is the names of the kings and some copies of wheat contracts.”

Our narrator, the omniscient and no-nonsense Stage Manager, is portrayed by Jim Parsons. Though lacking the proper gravitas for the role (especially if compared to prior Broadway runs featuring a 78-year-old Paul Newman in 2003 and the ageless Spalding Gray in 1989), Wilder’s turn of phrase steers Parsons through deep waters, inducing tears as he observes, “This is the way we were: in our growing up and in our marrying and in our living and in our dying.”

Love is more an ideal than a passion in Our Town so if Zoey Deutch as Emily and Ephraim Sykes as George lack a certain spark it only serves to underscore how emotions can be taken for granted until it is too late to act upon them. Circling around the young couple, the capable supporting cast includes Julie Halston, displaying her always keen sense of humor in the chatty role of Mrs. Soames, a fine Donald Webber, Jr. as the troubled choir director, Simon Stimson, Richard Thomas, deep in his wheelhouse as the folksy and smart father of Emily, and John McGinty, a deaf actor who adds a hundred shades of complexity to the usually thankless role of Howie Newsome, the milkman. Meanwhile, the romance between George’s parents (Billy Eugene Jones and Michelle Wilson) is never less than touching and very nearly crushing when, late in the play, the widower doctor lays flowers at his wife’s grave, as she looks on from beyond.

The design team is on point with the masterful scenic designer Beowulf Boritt teaming with lighting designer Allen Lee Hughes to create a stunning cloud of floating, softly glowing lanterns that stretch from the town cemetery, up and past the proscenium and out into the house where they hang over the audience like the ghosts of ancestors. There are so many townsfolk to look at and so many ideas to linger over here, but the ultimate irony of this production is that it feels rushed. Hurrying to get three acts into 105 minutes, Leon’s pacing is often breathless and time, despite what Wilder tries to teach us, zooms past in a flurry.

 

Our Town – By Thornton Wilder, directed by Kenny Leon

WITH: Jim Parsons (Stage Manager), Zoey Deutch (Emily Webb), Katie Holmes (Mrs. Webb), Billy Eugene Jones (Dr. Gibbs), Ephraim Sykes (George Gibbs), Richard Thomas (Mr. Webb), Michelle Wilson (Mrs. Gibbs), Julie Halston (Mrs. Soames), Donald Webber, Jr. (Simon Stimson), Ephie Aardema Sarnak, Heather Ayers, Willa Bost, Bobby Daye, Safiya Kaijya Harris, Doron JéPaul, Shyla Lefner, Anthony Michael Lopez, John McGinty, Bryonha Marie, Kevyn Morrow, Hagan Oliveras, Noah Pyzik, Sky Smith, Bill Timoney, Ricardo Vázquez, Matthew Elijah Webb, Greg Wood and Nimene Sierra Wureh.

Scenic design by Beowulf Boritt, costume design by Dede Ayite, lighting design by Allen Lee Hughes, sound design by Justin Ellington, hair, wig & makeup design by J. Jared Janas. The Barrymore Theatre, 243 West 47th St., 212-239-6200, OurTownBroadway.com. Through January 19. Running time: 1 hour, 45 minutes

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

From the Burne-Jone-esque promotional photo of flower children lying in the grass, I thought Honeyland, currently playing at the Triad Theater, was going to be a nostalgic, illuminating musical representation of America’s 1960’s counterculture.  Alas, this show is anything else but.  The artwork promises Woodstock but Honeyland delivers summer stock.

Honeyland attempts to walk the line between serious and fun, and as a result doesn’t succeed on either level, despite the admirable efforts of a talented, committed cast.   The show suffers from  ‘too many stories, too little curation’ syndrome.  It’s actually at least three plays, only one of which is really interesting (Hint:  Vietnam and the loss of innocence.)

As a result,  the show meanders through a hodgepodge of awkward musical vignettes strung together with minimal, unprepossessing narration — and then it ends in 1969, right when the 60’s have hit their stride.  How could you leave the Summer of Love on the proverbial cutting room floor?!  I mean if you’re going to talk “turn on, tune in, drop out” and Vietnam, you gotta talk psychedelics and communes.  You gotta talk love-ins and flower power.  You gotta talk DMZ and Nixon.  Especially since the opening number is devoted to Vietnam.  One reference to Napalm just won’t do.

Beginning with a strong solo by romantic hero and soldier Mike (a sympathetic, vulnerable Ben James Tyrrell) singing of his fear and desperation, the first impression is we’re going to watch a sensitive examination of the terrible human cost of war.  Dreams dashed, lives wasted.  Strong stuff, hugely ambitions but equally hugely relevant and ripe with promise.  That’s play #1.

We move to the backstory and the people left behind.  Mike leads a group of idealistic young artists exploring black box, avant-garde performance.   There is the inevitable backstage drama.  However, the writers draw the merest of sketches of the conflict between Mike and Tom (a stalwart Jacob Higdon) vying for the affections of ingenue Helen (an appealing Anika Buchanan).  Perennial third wheel Fran (Abby Goldberg, whose sparkle will not be denied) referees as she narrates.  (One script note:  Fran refers to Mike gigging at cafe on Auburn St.  in Cambridge.  It’s actually Mount Auburn St.)  When Mike leaves, their relationships fracture.  That’s play #2.

Framing the musical in flashback does not work because the material subsequent to the first scene lacks the emotional heft to support the set-up.  That said, there are some snappy numbers, particularly “When I Grow Up” and “60’s Girls” which are upbeat and include much needed choreography, which briefly brings the stage alive.  For a moment the actors throw off the self-conscious shackles of the requirement to Be Very Meaningful, giving us all a chance to breathe.  These numbers also convey more about each character than the tin-eared dialogue and emotionless narration.

For all of the internal conflict, the show feels a bit lifeless.  Instead of directing, Denny Lawrence relies on the weak material to do the work, leaving the actors hanging in the breeze.  If Lawrence is not going to draw clear lines or build a narrative, he could at least make better use of the upstage projection screen.  It’s the one tool he has by which to expand the limited stage space.  For instance, maybe open up the travel song with some ‘on-the-road again’ footage, or flash a series of groovy Laugh-In artwork.  Similarly, Ben Hostetler’s lighting feels mostly one-dimensional.  Lots of abrupt, white lights-up/lights-down.  A little color would add much needed shape to the Triad Theater’s cramped space.  And why use the dramatic lighting effects in the first scene so sparingly?  In addition, the show is too loud.  The sound balance is sometimes so off it is frequently difficult to hear the either song or dialogue.

Writers Clarry Evans and Denny Lawrence need to address the musical’s structure, as in they need actually to create one.  But how?  The two lovely acoustic songs Ben James Tyrrell sings offer a big clue, by which I mean the whole clue.  These solos draw more conclusions than the rest of the show.  And you can actually hear Tyrrell’s beautiful voice.  Evans and Lawrence also need to make a basic decision regarding the direction of the score.  Will it move stylistically with the culture, e.g., from “Where the Boys Are” to “Let the Sunshine In,” or will the music flow in a consistent style, reflecting change but not being part of it.

A ruthless restructure, cutting away the chaff and at least 1/3 of the music, and focusing on character would help this piece enormously.  Give these actors something to work with.  And for the love of Heaven, cut the cringe worthy marijuana sequence.  Such scenes almost always fail.  Please.  Just say no.

I really wanted to like Honeyland, perhaps in a fit of nostalgia for a time that held its many dangers, but also represented a moment when youthful idealism fueled Bohemian flower children to fight for civil rights and against the war.  The positive change civil disobedience can inspire is very real.  It can save a country from becoming its worst self.   Sorry, I’ve veered into play #3.

Honeyland, music by Clarry Evans and book by Denny Lawrence.  Directed by Denny Lawrence.  With Anika Buchanon, Abby Goldberg, Jacob Higdon and Ben James Tyrrell.

Lighting Design by Ben Hostetler, costume design by Molly Goldbreg, sound design by Ben Hosatetler.  Choreographed by Michelle Lemon.

At the Triad Theater (158 West 72nd Street) through November 2nd.  For tickets go to The Triad Theater.  Runtime:  75 minutes, no intermission.

excerpt.rendered: From the Burne-Jone-esque promotional photo I thought Honeyland was going to be a nostalgic, romantic, perhaps insightful musical representation of 1960’s counterculture.  I’m sorry to say, but this show is anything else but.  The artwork promises Woodstock but alas Honeyland gives summer stock. Much like a Bohemian maxi dress, the rudderless material leaves the actors hanging in the breeze.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“Please silence your cell phones. The game is about to start.” Comes over the loudspeakers in the gym. And then the lights dim.

There’s a basketball game being played at La MaMa right now using a ball filled with blood. The blood of those beaten and tortured by the current Belarus regime. It’s a gut-wrenching visual that covers the lead actress (who’s personal story this is) as she discovers what’s been hidden in the thing she has built her whole life around, a relationship with a ball called Mr. Spalding.

KS6: Small Forward is the personal story of European basketball star (Katsiaryna Snytsina (Katya), playing herself), how she came to play basketball growing up in Belarus, then moving on to make a name for herself on the international courts, and culminating in the choice she made to leave basketball to become the political activist she is today, “The air of freedom is more important that the air to breathe.” KS6: Small Forward is both a life story and a protest.

With the set being an actual half-court basketball floor, a live DJ, projection screens, and live cameras, the 90-minute show doesn’t slow down for a second, even during half-time. The show is a little bit circus and a little bit spectacle, as sporting events are, with mascots, half-time shows, and rousing audience participation. This spectacle is all riding on the coming to terms with what is happening in one’s country and the lack of freedom living under a dictator. A warning for what could happen here as no one is immune.

Katya’s story was adapted for the stage by Belarus Free Theatre‘s (BFT) co-founders Nicolai Khalezin and Natalia Kaliada and was the opening choice for La MaMa’s 63rd season. BFT is banned in Belarus as they, as all theater should, hold the mirror up too closely to the world around them and the regime considers them a political threat. Knowing that you could never go home again, for fear of being arrested, adds a power and immediacy to what one creates.

Katya, performing as herself, seems to have stepped easily into acting and communicating with an audience. She is personable, open, and approachable, immediately creating a rapport between actor and spectator, now giving her all to something that has no final buzzer.

—–

Running until October 13 at the Ellen Stewart Theatre (66 E. 4 St.). Tickets HERE.

KS6: Small Forward is performed by: Katya Snytsina, Blanka Barbara, Darya Andreyanov, Mikalai Kuprych, and Raman Shytsko.

Set design is by Nicolai Khalezin, light design by Peter Small, video design by Dmytro Guk, movement direction by Janier De Frutos (also choreography consultant), choreography by Anthony Matsena, and sound design and original music by Blanka Barbara.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

“Is it too late now to say sorry?”  Justin Bieber croons at the close of Deep History, as the audience steps out of the dark theater and into the cool, crisp night air.  What are we apologizing for?  The variety of climate events and the actions that have gotten us to this place; a place where our bodies contain plastics and our air is mostly C02.

But is it hopeless? David Finnigan’s solo show asks.  Can we learn from the past to improve the future?  Can theater impact society’s outlook on climate change? Can we have hope and positivity in light of the impending “apocalypse”?

Finnigan has deep personal connections to climate science, with a father who was an early climate pioneer and began speaking of global warming in the late 80’s when journalists were more skeptical of the idea.  Inspired by his father’s request in late 2019 to help turn a series of notes into a book, Finnigan digs deeply into previous historical climate crises, under the assumption that – if humans are an adolescent species, we can learn from our past mistakes.  While Deep History may explore humans as adolescent, Finnigan is astutely self aware and the piece wields the depth and emotional maturity of one much older and wiser. 

Deep History truly begins to shine as Finnigan’s experiment unravels and the actual lessons from who we were and how we got here are uncovered.  Finnigan reveals that while there may not be an apocalypse for the whole of humankind, we are sure to experience personal apocalypses in the coming months – if we haven’t already been subjected to them.

David Finnigan;
photo by Joan Marcus

Playing in the Shiva black box space at the Public, Deep History feels almost like walking into a lecture.  A phone camera is set to record across a black tablecloth-laden table on one side and a second table hosts a computer set to operate the projector onto the large blank screen at the back of the space (video design by Hayley Egan).  A repurposed wall flat sits next to this table with a large panel of brown paper and a large sharpie.  However, the piece begins with an exploration of Finnigan’s top three songs of 2019, allowing the audience to breathe out a collective sigh of relief – this lecture will approach its lesson through humanity, not statistics.

A combination history lesson, personal journey, and allegory, Deep History urges us to care and to fight through both paralyzing facts and charming soliloquies.  It scares us just enough and encourages us just enough to maybe, hopefully be the change we want to see in the world; to make the world a better place and truly learn from the human mis-steps that got us here with the promise that: maybe down the road, our great-great grandchildren may see the other side of this climate crises and live in a world that progresses toward better than before.  After all, humans have been surviving for thousands of years: adapting, rebuilding, expanding.

 

DEEP HISTORY – written and performed by David Finnigan

Video design by Hayley Egan; music by Reuben Ingall; direction by Annette Mees; production stage management by Buzz Cohen; line producer, Citali Pizarro; company manager, Heather Fighthorn; production management, Aliyah Sall.  Presented by the Public Theater: Oskar Eustis, artistic director, Patrick Willingham, executive director.  Through November 10.  https://publictheater.org/productions/season/2425/deep-history

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“What is a song? A song is a dream… a place to be. Somewhere you can live. And in that place, there are no walls. No boundaries. No locks. No keys. You can go anywhere…”

Back in the mid-50s their widowed mother (Laura Donnelly) attempted to turn her four daughters into a successful singing group, a-la the Andrew’s Sisters, in order to give them more of the prizes of life that she had been denied. Despite that want, a song is still only a dream and when reality rings the wake-up alarm there’s life to contend with.

The alarm has long since gone off, it’s 20 years later, 1976 in Blackpool, England, and three sisters (will the fourth show?) reunite as their mother lay dying upstairs in their home and business, the Seaview Luxury Guesthouse and Spa (neither in view of the sea, luxurious, or a spa). The play flips back and forth between these two eras as we witness the repercussions and hard truths of life’s decisions and unhealed childhood trauma and wounds that festered and framed the adults the sisters have become.

The Hills of California (California symbolising a better life) is a strong story about sisters, how we never grow up, we never leave home, and how impulsive choices of the past can fester and overshadow our whole lives. A very good Broadway drama that will leave you more than satisfied with having spent time at the Seaview.

The intimacy of such a story, despite its cast of 17, is well directed by Sam Mendes on a rotating set by Rob Howell of the guesthouse’s common parlor space with tiki bar and juke box, and spins on the other side to reveal the family’s private kitchen. The turntable is well used as it melds the passing of time and staying still all at once. It is hovered over by a humongous rotating Hogwarts type staircase that just keeps going up level upon level.

All the cast is great (highlighted by Laura Donnelly double-cast as mother and daughter) and the story will remind you of the family travails in August: Osage County and just as memorable.

—–

The Hills of California, written by Jez Butterworth and directed by Sam Mendes.

The cast: Laura Donnelly as Joan/Veronica; Leanne Best as Gloria; Ophelia Lovibond as Ruby; Helena Wilson as Jill; Nancy Allsop as Young Gloria; Sophia Ally as Young Ruby; Lara McDonnell as Young Joan; and Nicola Turner as Young Jill.

And includes Bryan Dick, Richard Short, David Wilson Barnes, Richard Lumsden, Ta’Rea Campbell, Sawyer Barth, Ellyn Heald, Cameron Scoggins, and Max Roll.

Creative team includes Rob Howell (designer), Natasha Chivers (lighting design), Nick Powell (composer, sound design, and arrangements), Ellen Kane (choreography), Campbell Young (wigs, hair & makeup design), Candida Caldicot (musical supervision and arrangements), Kate Wilson (dialect coach).

The running time is a short 2 hours and 45 minutes (not being facetious), including a 15-minute intermission after Act One and a 2-minute pause after Act Two.

The Broadhurst Theatre (235 W. 44th Street, between 7th Ave 8th Ave). Tickets can be had HERE.

title.rendered: Bill Russell – Divas I Love Singing Lyrics I Wrote

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

In a special performance at Birdland on September 30th, celebrated lyricist Bill Russell showcased some of his most famous songs from his long career.   Lean and vibrant, Russell burst with positive energy.  It is clear he loves his work and appreciates the talent of his singers.   In Divas I Love Singing Lyrics I Wrote four of Russell’s favorite ‘divas’ shared stage with him:  Christiane Noll (standing in for an ailing Lillias White), Alice Ripley, Erin Davie, and Charity Angél Dawson.

The program opened with a touching song from Elegies for Aging Punks and Raging Queens (music by Janet Hood), which was first produced in 1989.  Alice Ripley, who created the leading role of Violet Hilton in the original production of Side Show sang with affecting simplicity.  “Angels, Punks and Raging Queens” evokes images of a grittier, yet more innocent New York City – an innocence we soon lost as the AIDS epidemic tightened its merciless grip on the gay community.  Everyone lost someone.  Later in the cabaret Erin Davie brought us to tears with another song from that show, “My Brother Lived in San Francisco.”

In his patter throughout the evening, Russell offered various peeks behind the theatrical curtain, revealing some of the nuts and bolts of how a show makes it from page to stage.  For instance, the saga of the original opening number for Side Show, one of several collaborations with composer Henry Krieger.  The song was out; it was in; it was out again, not because it was not good, but because as the show evolved over time, the opening number no longer fit.  Erin Davie, who played Violet in the show’s revival, sang “Sideshow” mellifluously with an easy intuition and clarity..  Davie also unwittingly gave us the kind of unique moment you can only experience in live theater.  She went up on a lyric (something that has happened to every singer ever in the history of singing).  Like a pro she stopped the song, bashfully announced a need to start again, and then performed the song beautifully.

In a quicksilver change from wistful to brazen, Davie then dove into “Bankin’ on Jesus” a rollicking up tempo from the show Pageant (music by Albert Evans).  It is always interesting to hear a song in a new voice.  Pageant is a musical performed by men.  Davie delighted in this in this brash send-up of Holy Rollers.  In another role reversal, Charity Angél Dawson, currently performing in & Juliet on Broadway, lent her powerful voice to a male solo “All in the Mind” written for the revival of Side Show.  Later in the evening Dawson also sang a heartfelt interpretation of “Your Show is Going On” (music by Henry Krieger) from the 1993 Easter Bonnet competition.

In a last-minute cameo appearance, Christiane Noll lit up the stage with “Let’s Stay Out and Play” from Kept (music by Henry Krieger), a musical interpretation of Camille.  Noll delivered a strong belt sound, but in the subsequent banter with Russell, she off handedly tossed off some gorgeous coloratura notes, and I thought: Yes!  Give us more of that, please!  For in truth,the evening’s music, while engaging throughout, began to run together somewhat.  After a while I found myself pining for a different vocal color.  So much of what I heard felt as if it was in the same key, landing squarely in the most challenging part of the voice, the break between chest and head voice.  This was particularly the case in “Who Will Love Me as I Am” from Sideshow.

In a change of pace, Musical Director Mark Hartman performed “I’d Rather be a Fairy Than a Troll” from Fourtune (music by Ron Melrose), a very gay, very farcical farce, as in lyrics like “I’d rather be a fairy/be extraordinary”  In addition to delivering as a singer, Hartman also played some fantastic jazz piano.  He and the band, drummer Jeff Potter and bassist John Loehrke played with consistent excellence throughout.

And before we knew it, it was time to go.  After a program of musical tenderness and mischief, the stirring song “I Will Never Leave You” from Side Show closed out the evening perfectly.  In their shimmering dresses in shades of gold and bronze, Ripley, Davie and Dawson poured their hearts into this uplifting farewell.

Divas I Love Singing Lyrics I Wrote with Alice Ripley, Erin Davie, Christiane Noll and Charity Angél Dawson.   Mark Hartman on piano, Jeff Potter on drums, and John Loehrke on bass.   Birdland Jazz Club located at 315 West 44th Street (between 8th and 9th Avenues) in Manhattan.
