@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

title.rendered: The Wind and the Rain: A story about Sunny’s Bar

content.rendered:
By David Walters

How do you write a play about time?

Here’s how.

The Wind and the Rain: A story about Sunny’s Bar, is the answer to that how.

Playwright Sarah Gancher has distilled the history of time on a piece of ground that is Red Hook, Brooklyn into a little over two-hour play (more like an experience than a conventional play). The story centers on a bar, Sunny’s, on the end of Conover Street that has been there, like, forever.

Before you even get there, it’s an adventure to go see this play as public transportation (subway to bus, or ferry and walk) is few and far between, so you’ll have to plan. The journey to get there only adds to the magic of what you will experience, I swear.

The play begins on a piece of history that is a restored barge which is the basis of The Waterfront Museum.  The setting of worn timbers and the rocking of the boat from waves off of the harbor immediately transports the audience (that sits in chairs in a circle around a performance space) back in time. Four actors, Jennifer Regan, Pete Simpson, Paco Tolson, Jen Tullock (each one is superb in all the characters they portray as well as the palpable joy they bring in what they’re doing), begin the evening of enthralling storytelling by setting the stage of what we are about to embark on, seeing through time. They will represent hundreds of people who have tread on this piece of Brooklyn and left their mark on the land. We meet Sunny as a youth, his ancestors, and share how he and his partner Tone (pronounced tuna) Johansen came to be. Using the event of hurricane Sandy that wiped out much of the area, we then bounce back and forth in time (and occasionally are in two eras at once) as the history of Sunny’s bar comes floating up in the detritus of the storm’s destruction. Utilizing projections and audience involvement the play creates a sense of community that is the basis of what the bar has always been. The story culminates in a short journey as the cast, musicians, and audience leave the barge and pilgrimage to the front of Sunny’s bar a short walk away, where we experience a projection of the people who have also walked and lived lives on that spot through the ages.

This is a magical site-specific play, in a historical setting, that will leave you smarter than when you walked in and with more understanding and respect for lives lived that have gone on before you.

Highly, highly recommended.

—–

The Wind and the Rain: A story about Sunny’s Bar, written by Sarah Gancher, directed by Jared Mezzocchi, and presented by En Garde Arts in association with The Vineyard.

The cast includes Jennifer Regan, Pete Simpson, Paco Tolson, Jen Tullock, musician Pete Lanctot, Sunday night special guests were Stan Baum on guitar, Erik Alvar on mandolin, and everyone in the audience.

Designers: Marcelo Martinez Garcia, scenic design; Mika Eubanks, costume design; Amith Chandrashaker, lighting design; Jane Shaw, sound design; Paul Deziel, projection design; Thomas Jenkeleit, props design.

Now through October 27. Tickets HERE.

I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

title.rendered: The Phenomenal, Marvelous Marilyn Maye at 54 Below

content.rendered:
By Betsyann Faiella

The marvelous Marilyn Maye looked particularly glamorous on Oct.1st at 54 Below.

She seemed to glitter in gold from head to toe, as she entered with her opening number, “The Song is You” (Music by Jerome Kern and Lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II). She followed that with “It’s A Most Unusual Day” (Music by Jimmy McHugh and Lyrics by Harold Adamson) and the first half of her wonderful show was mainly high energy, up-tempo, including a Fats Waller medley featuring the naughty “I Want A Little Sugar in My Bowl.”

I can’t leave out the off the cuff comedy riff that preceded it, though, about National Cookie Day. Imagine Marilyn Maye baking cookies…no, I can’t, and neither can she. It was hilarious, she took her time, and engaged the audience fully in the joke. She had some trouble holding her medley of “Fly Me to the Moon” (Bart Howard) and “Come Fly With Me” (Music by Jimmy Van Heusen and Lyrics by Sammy Cahn) together, but bluffed and laughed her way through – making up some lyrics and employing gibberish at other times.

In absolutely great spirits, she entertained an audience eager to be there and eager to lavish her with love, as she does in return. As the show continued, after her homage to Ray Charles, she settled into a second half of mainly ballads and treated the audience to “Bye Bye Country Boy” (Music and Lyrics by Blossom Dearie and Jack Segal), a song we don’t hear enough since Blossom left the building.

Hearing Marilyn sing her most adored numbers, including “Ribbons Down My Back” (Jerry Herman), “Fifty Percent” (Music by Billy Goldenberg, Lyrics by Alan Bergman and Marilyn Bergman), and “Guess Who I Saw Today” (Music and Lyrics by Murray Grand) is thrilling and heartbreaking at once, and these favorites elicited standing ovations and tears. There were two Broadway stars sitting adjacent to me and the looks on their faces after hearing her absolutely kill on “Fifty Percent” were priceless. Marilyn’s interpretation of the song is always a quiet performance, the story of a married lover, that she alternates with speak-singing and singing. Each Broadway star seemed to be asking themselves, “what just happened here?” Knocked out.

There were no high kicks in this show. But there was plenty of great material, planned and spontaneous, hot rhythms, fun and the usual incredible musicianship of her band: Music Director and Pianist Tedd Firth, Bassist Tom Hubbard, and Drummer Mark McLean. They never fail to amaze.

Marilyn Maye closed her show with a couple of tributes to …life. In one, she sings, “The secret of life is enjoying the passage of time…,” (“The Secret of Life” by James Taylor) in the other she sings, “and even though I’m satisfied I’m hungry still, to see what’s down another road beyond the hill, and do it all again…” (“Here’s to Life” with Music by Artie Butler and Lyrics by Phyllis Molinary).

Words to live by. Marilyn Maye certainly does.

Marilyn Maye is an entertainer, the likes of which we will never, ever, see again. If you haven’t experienced her, she has several more engagements in 2024 at 54 below: Oct 10, 11, 12, 23, 29 and Nov. 13, 24, 25.

For tickets, visit: https://54below.org/
